concept_name: Cardiac looping and left-right dynein defect (Kartagener syndrome)
stem: A 28-year-old man presents for evaluation of infertility after 2 years of unsuccessful attempts to conceive. He has had chronic sinusitis and a productive cough since childhood, and sweat chloride testing at age 6 was normal. Examination shows heart sounds that are loudest in the right fifth intercostal space. Semen analysis shows a normal sperm count with immotile spermatozoa, and chest CT shows bronchiectasis with the cardiac apex and stomach bubble on the right. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?
option_A: Defective left-right dynein function in motile cilia
option_B: Failed migration of neural crest cells into the outflow tract
option_C: Nonfusion of septum primum and septum secundum
option_D: Incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions of the AV canal
option_E: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
correct_explanation: Chronic sinopulmonary disease with bronchiectasis, immotile sperm, and a normal sweat chloride test indicates primary ciliary dyskinesia, and the addition of dextrocardia with a right-sided stomach bubble makes this Kartagener syndrome. The primary heart tube loops during week 4 to establish left-right polarity, and this process depends on motile ciliary flow. Left-right dynein is the axonemal motor protein that powers ciliary beating, so a defect randomizes laterality and produces dextrocardia or situs inversus. The same immotile cilia fail to clear mucus from the respiratory tract, causing recurrent sinusitis and bronchiectasis. Sperm flagella share the same axonemal structure, which explains the male infertility. First Aid lists the dynein defect under cardiac looping on p. 284.

B.reason: Neural crest migration forms the truncal and bulbar ridges, so its failure produces conotruncal defects such as TGA, tetralogy of Fallot, and persistent truncus. It does not alter the position of the heart or impair ciliary motility. This patient has no cyanosis or congenital outflow lesion.

C.reason: Nonfusion of septum primum and secundum leaves a patent foramen ovale, which is usually asymptomatic and found in about 25% of people. It does not explain dextrocardia, bronchiectasis, or immotile sperm.

D.reason: Incomplete endocardial cushion fusion produces an AV septal defect and is associated with Down syndrome. The resulting lesion causes heart failure in infancy, which is not described here, and it does not rotate the heart to the right.

E.reason: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral causes D-transposition of the great arteries, which presents with cyanosis in the first days of life. This patient reached adulthood without cyanosis and has chronic airway disease.

high_yield_pearl: Dextrocardia plus sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and immotile sperm means a dynein defect (Kartagener syndrome).
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Cardiac looping begins in week 4 and establishes left-right polarity; a left-right dynein defect can cause dextrocardia, as in Kartagener syndrome.
• Clinical Findings: Situs inversus or dextrocardia, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, infertility from immotile sperm.
• Diagnostics: Chest imaging showing dextrocardia; normal sweat chloride; abnormal ciliary function.
• Management: Airway clearance and treatment of recurrent infections; complications include bronchiectasis and infertility.

concept_name: Outflow tract formation and conotruncal abnormalities (persistent truncus arteriosus)
stem: A 4-day-old boy born to a mother with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes is cyanotic and tachypneic. Oxygen saturation is 78% on room air and 80% after 100% oxygen. Examination shows a single loud S2 and a systolic ejection click at the left sternal border. Echocardiography shows a single arterial trunk with one semilunar valve overriding a large VSD, and the pulmonary arteries arise directly from the trunk. Which of the following embryologic failures best explains this lesion?
option_A: Failure of neural crest-derived truncal and bulbar ridges to form the aorticopulmonary septum
option_B: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
option_C: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
option_D: Incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions of the AV canal
option_E: Defective left-right dynein function during cardiac looping
correct_explanation: A single arterial trunk with one semilunar valve and a VSD in the infant of a diabetic mother is persistent truncus arteriosus. Neural crest cells migrate into the outflow tract to form the truncal and bulbar ridges, which spiral and fuse into the aorticopulmonary septum. This septum divides the truncus arteriosus into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. When the ridges fail to form and fuse, a single common trunk remains, which receives blood from both ventricles through the VSD. The resulting mixing causes cyanosis that does not correct with 100% oxygen. First Aid lists persistent truncus among the conotruncal abnormalities on p. 284.

B.reason: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral produces D-transposition of the great arteries with two separate, switched vessels. This infant has a single trunk, so the septum failed to divide the outflow tract at all.

C.reason: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum causes tetralogy of Fallot, with pulmonary stenosis, an overriding aorta, VSD, and RVH. Two separate great vessels are present in that condition, whereas this infant has a single trunk.

D.reason: Incomplete endocardial cushion fusion causes an AV septal defect with a common AV valve, typically in Down syndrome. The semilunar valves and great vessels are separate in that disorder, so it would not produce one arterial trunk.

E.reason: A dynein defect disturbs left-right polarity, causing dextrocardia and Kartagener syndrome. It would not create a truncal anomaly, and this infant lacks respiratory disease or abnormal heart position.

high_yield_pearl: Failure of neural crest migration gives the conotruncal trio: TGA, tetralogy of Fallot, and persistent truncus.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Neural crest cell migrations form the truncal and bulbar ridges, which spiral and fuse to form the aorticopulmonary septum and then the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Failure causes TGA, tetralogy of Fallot, and persistent truncus arteriosus.
• Clinical Findings: Early cyanosis; truncus is associated with a VSD and with maternal diabetes and 22q11 syndromes.
• Diagnostics: Echocardiography showing a single arterial trunk.
• Management: Surgical repair; prostaglandins may maintain ductal flow in other cyanotic lesions.

concept_name: Valve development and valve anomalies (Ebstein anomaly)
stem: A 3-day-old boy has mild cyanosis. His mother took lithium throughout pregnancy for bipolar disorder. Examination shows a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and chest radiograph shows marked cardiomegaly. ECG shows a short PR interval with a delta wave. Echocardiography shows apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet toward the right ventricular apex with right-to-left atrial shunting through a patent foramen ovale. Which of the following best describes the valve anomaly?
option_A: Downward displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets into the right ventricle
option_B: Complete absence of the tricuspid valve with a hypoplastic right ventricle
option_C: Fusion of the pulmonary valve cusps causing outflow obstruction
option_D: Cleft anterior mitral leaflet with a primum atrial septal defect
option_E: Bicuspid aortic valve with juxtaductal coarctation
correct_explanation: Prenatal lithium exposure, tricuspid regurgitation, cardiomegaly, and an accessory pathway with a delta wave identify Ebstein anomaly. Mitral and tricuspid valves normally derive from the fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal, and First Aid notes that valvular anomalies may be stenotic, regurgitant, atretic, or displaced. In Ebstein anomaly the tricuspid leaflets are displaced downward into the right ventricle, which artificially atrializes the upper portion of the ventricle. The functional right ventricle is small, and the regurgitant tricuspid valve raises right atrial pressure, producing right-to-left shunting across a patent foramen ovale and cyanosis. Accessory conduction pathways cause the preexcitation pattern.

B.reason: Tricuspid atresia is an absent tricuspid valve with a hypoplastic right ventricle and requires an ASD and a VSD or PDA for survival. The ECG typically shows left axis deviation with tall P waves, and this infant has a tricuspid valve that is present but displaced, with regurgitation.

C.reason: Pulmonary valve stenosis obstructs right ventricular outflow and causes a systolic ejection murmur, not a holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation. It would not cause apical displacement of the tricuspid leaflet or a delta wave.

D.reason: A cleft mitral valve with a primum ASD results from incomplete endocardial cushion fusion and causes mitral regurgitation, typically in Down syndrome. The echocardiogram in this patient shows a displaced tricuspid valve, and the history involves lithium exposure.

E.reason: Bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation are associated with Turner syndrome and cause upper extremity hypertension with weak femoral pulses. They do not cause cardiomegaly with a displaced tricuspid valve or an accessory pathway.

high_yield_pearl: Maternal lithium plus tricuspid regurgitation and a delta wave means Ebstein anomaly.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Aortic and pulmonary valves derive from the endocardial cushions of the outflow tract; mitral and tricuspid valves from the fused cushions of the AV canal. Anomalies can be stenotic, regurgitant, atretic (tricuspid atresia), or displaced (Ebstein anomaly, which can follow in utero lithium exposure).
• Clinical Findings: Ebstein anomaly: tricuspid regurgitation, accessory conduction pathways, right-sided HF; rare.
• Diagnostics: Echocardiography showing apical displacement of the tricuspid leaflet and an atrialized RV.
• Management: Treat arrhythmias and heart failure; surgical repair for severe disease.

concept_name: Septation of the atria and patent foramen ovale
stem: A 31-year-old scuba diver develops sudden vertigo, right arm numbness, and mottled skin shortly after a rapid ascent. Blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg and heart rate is 94/min, and S2 splits normally with respiration without a murmur. Transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline shows microbubbles crossing from the right to the left atrium during a Valsalva maneuver through a flap-like opening in the atrial septum. No persistent gap in the septum is seen at rest. The one-way valve at this site is derived from which of the following embryonic structures?
option_A: Remnant of septum primum
option_D: Right horn of the sinus venosus
correct_explanation: A transient right-to-left shunt across a flap that opens only with straining, with a normal S2 split and no persistent septal gap, identifies a patent foramen ovale, here causing paradoxical gas embolism. The septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions, and the ostium secundum forms in it by cell death. The septum secundum then develops to the right of septum primum and covers most of the ostium secundum, leaving the foramen ovale. The remaining portion of septum primum forms the one-way valve of the foramen ovale. After birth, higher LA pressure presses the valve against the septum secundum, and the two normally fuse, but fusion fails in about 25% of people. This is detailed on p. 284.

B.reason: The septum secundum is the thick, rigid rim on the right side that frames the foramen ovale, and it does not act as the flap valve. The valve is the remaining portion of septum primum, which is why the flap moves with pressure changes.

C.reason: The endocardial cushions contribute to the atrial septum, the membranous interventricular septum, and the AV valves. They are not the source of the flap valve of the foramen ovale, and cushion defects cause AV septal defects.

D.reason: The right horn of the sinus venosus forms the smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum). It does not contribute to the interatrial septum.

E.reason: The primitive atrium forms the trabeculated parts of both atria and not the septal flap. The flap arises from septum primum tissue.

high_yield_pearl: The flap valve of the foramen ovale is the remnant of septum primum.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Septum primum grows toward the cushions; ostium secundum forms in it by cell death; septum secundum covers the ostium secundum, leaving the foramen ovale. After birth, higher LA pressure closes the flap and the two septa fuse in infancy or early childhood. Failure to fuse leaves a PFO (about 25% of people).
• Clinical Findings: Usually asymptomatic; paradoxical emboli.
• Diagnostics: Bubble-contrast echocardiography.
• Management: Treat the embolic source; closure in selected patients.

concept_name: Ventricular septation and ventricular septal defect
stem: A 6-week-old girl is brought for poor feeding and sweating during bottle feeds. She is at the 5th percentile for weight and her respirations are 52/min. Examination shows a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with a palpable thrill, no cyanosis, and a normal S2 split. Catheterization shows a step-up in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle, and echocardiography shows a defect in the membranous septum with an intact primum atrial septum and no cleft mitral valve. Which of the following developmental failures best explains this lesion?
option_A: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to rotate and fuse with the muscular interventricular septum
option_B: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
option_C: Incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions of the AV canal
option_D: Nonfusion of septum primum and septum secundum
option_E: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate to the outflow tract
correct_explanation: A harsh holosystolic murmur with a thrill, a right ventricular oxygen step-up, and a membranous septal defect indicate a VSD, the most common congenital cardiac anomaly. The muscular interventricular septum forms first, leaving the interventricular foramen. The aorticopulmonary septum then rotates and fuses with the muscular septum to form the membranous interventricular septum and close the foramen. Failure of this fusion leaves a membranous VSD, producing a left-to-right shunt that raises pulmonary blood flow. This accounts for the heart failure symptoms of tachypnea, sweating, and poor weight gain. Small defects often close spontaneously, but large defects can lead to Eisenmenger syndrome.

B.reason: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral causes D-transposition of the great arteries, which presents with early cyanosis. This infant is acyanotic and has a left-to-right shunt.

C.reason: Incomplete endocardial cushion fusion causes an AV septal defect, which includes a primum ASD and cleft mitral valve in the partial form and is associated with Down syndrome. Echocardiography here shows an intact primum septum and no cleft mitral valve.

D.reason: Nonfusion of septum primum and secundum leaves a patent foramen ovale, an atrial lesion that is usually asymptomatic. It does not produce a ventricular step-up or a holosystolic murmur.

E.reason: Failure of neural crest migration causes conotruncal defects with early cyanosis, such as truncus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot. This infant is not cyanotic and has an isolated membranous VSD.

high_yield_pearl: Membranous VSD is failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to fuse with the muscular septum.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: The muscular IV septum forms and leaves the interventricular foramen; the aorticopulmonary septum rotates and fuses with it to form the membranous septum. VSD is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly, usually membranous.
• Clinical Findings: Holosystolic harsh murmur at the tricuspid area; heart failure if large; O2 saturation increased in RV and pulmonary artery.
• Diagnostics: Echocardiography; oxygen step-up on catheterization.
• Management: Small defects often close spontaneously; large defects need surgery; untreated large defects can lead to Eisenmenger syndrome.

stem: A 7-month-old boy with trisomy 21 has failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory infections, and tachypnea at rest. Examination shows a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and a loud pulmonic component of S2. ECG shows a superior (leftward) QRS axis. Echocardiography shows a single common AV valve with both an atrial and a ventricular septal defect. Which of the following best explains this lesion?
option_A: Incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions
option_B: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to rotate and fuse with the muscular septum alone
option_C: Nonfusion of septum primum and septum secundum
option_D: Failure of neural crest cell migration
option_E: Excessive cell death in septum primum
correct_explanation: A common AV valve with both an ASD and a VSD in a child with Down syndrome is a complete AV septal defect. The endocardial cushions grow to separate the atria from the ventricles and contribute to atrial septation and the membranous portion of the interventricular septum. When the cushions fail to fuse completely, the septa and AV valves are defective, and in the complete form a common AV valve connects all four chambers. The large left-to-right shunt overloads the pulmonary circulation, causing failure to thrive and recurrent respiratory infections. The partial form has a primum ASD with a cleft mitral valve causing mitral regurgitation, with no VSD.

B.reason: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to fuse with the muscular septum causes an isolated membranous VSD. It does not create a common AV valve or an atrial defect.

C.reason: Nonfusion of septum primum and secundum produces a PFO, which does not cause a ventricular defect or a common AV valve. It is often asymptomatic.

D.reason: Neural crest failure causes outflow tract defects such as truncus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot, with early cyanosis. This infant has a defect at the AV canal level.

E.reason: Excessive cell death in septum primum would enlarge the ostium secundum and produce a secundum ASD. That would not create a ventricular defect or a common AV valve.

high_yield_pearl: Down syndrome plus a common AV valve means an endocardial cushion defect.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Endocardial cushions separate atria from ventricles and contribute to atrial septation and the membranous IV septum. Incomplete fusion causes AV septal defect (AV canal defect).
• Clinical Findings: Complete: common AV valve with ASD and VSD. Partial: primum ASD with cleft mitral valve causing MR, no VSD. Associated with Down syndrome.
• Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
• Management: Surgical repair; untreated shunts can lead to HF and pulmonary hypertension.

concept_name: Heart embryology: derivatives of cardinal veins (IVC)
stem: A 35-year-old man presents with right leg swelling and pain 4 days after a 12-hour flight. Temperature is 37.2°C, heart rate is 88/min, and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. Duplex ultrasonography shows a deep venous thrombosis of the right femoral vein. CT venography shows extension to the infrarenal inferior vena cava, and the interventional radiologist reviews the embryology of the vessel before planning filter placement. Which of the following embryonic structures give rise to the inferior vena cava?
option_A: Right common (anterior) cardinal vein
option_B: Posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins
option_C: Right horn of the sinus venosus
option_D: Left horn of the sinus venosus
correct_explanation: This is a deep venous thrombosis with proximal extension, so the clinical question is directed to the anatomy of the IVC. The inferior vena cava forms from the posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins. In contrast, the right common (anterior) cardinal vein forms the superior vena cava. The sinus venosus horns form the sinus venarum and the coronary sinus, and the primitive pulmonary vein forms the smooth part of the left atrium. Knowing these origins explains patterns of venous anomalies, such as the persistence of left-sided channels, that must be recognized before filter placement.

A.reason: The right common (anterior) cardinal vein forms the superior vena cava, which drains the upper body into the right atrium. The thrombus here involves the infrarenal IVC, which has a different origin.

B.reason: Correct answer

C.reason: The right horn of the sinus venosus forms the smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum). It does not form a systemic vein such as the IVC.

D.reason: The left horn of the sinus venosus forms the coronary sinus, which drains the heart wall. It is unrelated to the infrarenal IVC.

E.reason: The primitive pulmonary vein forms the smooth part of the left atrium where the pulmonary veins enter. It is unrelated to systemic venous drainage.

high_yield_pearl: Anterior cardinal gives SVC; posterior, sub-, and supracardinal veins give IVC.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Right common/anterior cardinal veins form the SVC; posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins form the IVC; right sinus horn forms the smooth RA; left sinus horn forms the coronary sinus; primitive pulmonary vein forms the smooth LA.
• Clinical Findings: Anomalies may be silent or affect catheter and filter placement.
• Diagnostics: CT or MR venography.
• Management: Anatomy guides line, filter, and surgical planning.

concept_name: Fetal-postnatal derivatives (urachus and median umbilical ligament)
stem: A 2-week-old boy has persistent clear, watery drainage from the umbilicus that increases when he cries. The umbilical stump separated at 10 days, and the periumbilical skin is mildly irritated. He is afebrile and feeds well. Ultrasonography shows a tubular tract from the dome of the bladder to the umbilicus, and drainage fluid has a high creatinine concentration. Persistence of which fetal structure explains this finding?
option_A: Allantois (urachus)
correct_explanation: Clear umbilical drainage with a high creatinine level and a tract from the bladder dome to the umbilicus indicates a patent urachus, with urine draining through the umbilicus. The urachus is the portion of the allantois that lies between the bladder and the umbilicus. It normally obliterates before birth and persists as the median umbilical ligament. Failure of obliteration produces a communication that leaks urine, which increases with crying because of the rise in intra-abdominal pressure. First Aid lists the allantois-to-urachus-to-median umbilical ligament sequence in the fetal-postnatal derivatives table.

B.reason: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis in the falciform ligament. Failure of its closure would cause bleeding or venous drainage, not urine with a high creatinine.

C.reason: The umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments after birth. They carry blood from the internal iliac arteries and do not communicate with the bladder.

D.reason: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum and shunts umbilical vein blood past the liver into the IVC. It is internal to the abdomen and does not communicate with the bladder.

E.reason: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum and connects the pulmonary artery with the aorta. A patent ductus causes a continuous murmur, not umbilical drainage.

high_yield_pearl: The urachus (allantois) becomes the median umbilical ligament; persistence leaks urine at the umbilicus.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Fetal structure to postnatal derivative: ductus arteriosus to ligamentum arteriosum; ductus venosus to ligamentum venosum; foramen ovale to fossa ovalis; allantois (urachus) to median umbilical ligament; umbilical arteries to medial umbilical ligaments; umbilical vein to ligamentum teres hepatis.
• Clinical Findings: Patent urachus: umbilical urine drainage.
• Diagnostics: Ultrasonography; fluid creatinine.
• Management: Surgical excision of the tract.

concept_name: Fetal circulation and changes at birth
stem: A term newborn girl is examined 10 minutes after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. She cried immediately, her heart rate is 150/min, respirations are 50/min, and oxygen saturation has risen from 70% to 95% over the first 10 minutes of life. The umbilical cord has been clamped and she is breathing spontaneously. Doppler echocardiography shows the flap of the foramen ovale closing against the atrial septum. Which of the following changes is the most direct cause of this closure?
option_A: Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance causing left atrial pressure to exceed right atrial pressure
option_B: Increased circulating prostaglandin E2 from the placenta
option_E: Increased flow through the ductus venosus
correct_explanation: In fetal life, high pulmonary vascular resistance and high right-sided pressures direct blood across the foramen ovale from the right to the left atrium. At birth, the infant takes a breath, which markedly reduces resistance in the pulmonary vasculature. Pulmonary blood flow and venous return to the left atrium rise, so left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure. This pressure reversal presses the septum primum flap against septum secundum and closes the foramen ovale, which becomes the fossa ovalis. The rise in oxygen and the fall in prostaglandins after placental separation likewise close the ductus arteriosus.

B.reason: Prostaglandins E1 and E2 keep the ductus arteriosus open, and their levels fall after placental separation. A rise would impede closure of the ductus rather than cause the foramen ovale to close.

C.reason: Increased fetal pulmonary resistance is the reason that blood is shunted across the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus in utero. Resistance falls after birth, and this fall causes the closure.

D.reason: Low oxygen tension helps keep the ductus arteriosus open, and the rise in oxygen after the first breath promotes ductal closure. This infant's oxygen saturation has increased, so the finding does not explain the closure.

E.reason: The ductus venosus shunts umbilical vein blood past the liver into the IVC and stops functioning when the cord is clamped. It does not affect the pressure relationship between the atria.

high_yield_pearl: The first breath lowers pulmonary resistance, raises LA pressure, and shuts the foramen ovale.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Fetal shunts: umbilical vein to ductus venosus to IVC; IVC blood to foramen ovale to LA; SVC blood to RV to pulmonary artery to ductus arteriosus to descending aorta (due to high fetal pulmonary resistance).
• Clinical Findings: At birth, a breath lowers pulmonary resistance and raises LA over RA pressure, closing the foramen ovale; increased O2 and decreased prostaglandins close the ductus.
• Diagnostics: Echocardiography confirms closure.
• Management: Persistent shunts (PDA, PFO) cause later disease.

concept_name: Patent ductus arteriosus: prostaglandins and NSAIDs
stem: A 2-day-old boy born to a mother with insulin-dependent diabetes is deeply cyanotic. Oxygen saturation is 68% and does not improve with 100% oxygen. Heart rate is 160/min, a single loud S2 is heard without a murmur, and chest radiograph shows a narrow mediastinum with an egg-on-a-string appearance. Echocardiography shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk arising from the left ventricle, with bidirectional shunting across a patent ductus arteriosus. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate bridge to surgical repair?
option_A: Alprostadil (prostaglandin E1)
correct_explanation: Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, an egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette, and an aorta arising from the right ventricle define D-transposition of the great arteries in an infant of a diabetic mother. The two circulations run in parallel, and survival depends on a shunt, such as the PDA, that allows mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Prostaglandins E1 and E2 keep the PDA open, so alprostadil (PGE1) is infused to maintain ductal patency until surgery. NSAIDs and acetaminophen inhibit prostaglandin synthesis and close the PDA, so they would be harmful. First Aid notes that PGE keeps the PDA open and that indomethacin ends it.

B.reason: Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and closes the PDA. Closing the duct in this infant would remove the only mixing site and could be fatal.

C.reason: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that closes a hemodynamically significant PDA in premature infants. In a cyanotic infant who depends on the shunt, closure would worsen hypoxemia.

D.reason: Acetaminophen also helps close the PDA by reducing prostaglandin synthesis. It is used for symptomatic PDA, not for ductal-dependent circulation.

E.reason: Digoxin is a positive inotrope that inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase and is used in heart failure and atrial fibrillation. It does not maintain ductal patency or improve mixing in TGA.

high_yield_pearl: PGE keeps the PDA open; indomethacin ends it.
topic_overview:
• Etiology/Pathophysiology: Closure of the ductus arteriosus follows increased O2 and decreased prostaglandins at birth. NSAIDs (indomethacin, ibuprofen) or acetaminophen help close a PDA, leaving the ligamentum arteriosum; PGE1 and PGE2 keep it open.
• Clinical Findings: Ductal-dependent lesions present with early cyanosis; D-TGA has an egg-on-a-string appearance.
• Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
• Management: Alprostadil to maintain the PDA until surgery in ductal-dependent lesions; NSAIDs to close a symptomatic PDA.

concept_name: Auscultation of the heart: murmur maneuvers (mitral valve prolapse)
stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with intermittent palpitations and atypical chest discomfort. She is thin, with a pulse of 78/min and blood pressure of 108/66 mm Hg. Auscultation at the apex while she is supine reveals a midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur that is loudest just before S2. Echocardiography confirms posterior displacement of the mitral leaflets into the left atrium with mild regurgitation. Which of the following maneuvers would move the click earlier in systole and lengthen the murmur?
option_A: Valsalva strain phase
correct_explanation: The midsystolic click and late systolic murmur are produced as the mitral leaflets prolapse into the left atrium and the chordae tendineae suddenly tense. The timing of the click depends on left ventricular volume: when the cavity is smaller, the leaflets prolapse earlier in systole. Valsalva strain and standing decrease venous return and preload, lowering LV volume, so the click moves earlier and the murmur lengthens. In contrast, maneuvers that raise LV volume, such as squatting or passive leg raise, delay the click and shorten the murmur. First Aid p. 294 lists MVP among the murmurs that become louder with standing and Valsalva, with an earlier midsystolic click.

B.reason: Squatting increases preload and afterload, which increases LV volume. A larger LV delays prolapse, so the click occurs later and the murmur is shorter.

C.reason: Passive leg raise increases venous return and LV volume, so the click is delayed. It would not shift the click earlier as the question requires.

D.reason: Handgrip greatly increases afterload and raises LV volume, which increases murmurs of MR, AR, and VSD but does not move an MVP click earlier. The enlarged ventricle would, if anything, delay the click.

E.reason: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart and decreases it to the left heart, so it mainly accentuates right-sided murmurs. It does not reliably change the timing of a left-sided mitral click.

high_yield_pearl: Decreased LV volume (standing, Valsalva) makes the MVP click earlier and the murmur longer.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Standing and Valsalva decrease preload and LV volume; passive leg raise increases preload; squatting increases preload and afterload; handgrip increases afterload. MVP click occurs earlier with decreased LV volume.
-  Clinical Findings: Midsystolic click with late crescendo systolic murmur loudest just before S2.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography; dynamic auscultation.
-  Management: Usually benign; MVP can predispose to infective endocarditis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has progressive fatigue, abdominal distension, and bilateral leg swelling 2 years after placement of a permanent transvenous pacemaker. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and heart rate is 72/min. A high-pitched holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border and increases with inspiration. Her liver is pulsatile and tender, and she has pitting edema to the knees. Which jugular venous pulse finding is most likely?
option_A: Absent x descent with a prominent v wave
correct_explanation: A holosystolic blowing murmur at the tricuspid area that increases with inspiration, a pulsatile liver, and right heart failure after pacemaker lead placement indicate tricuspid regurgitation. TR is often due to RV dilatation and can be secondary to permanent pacemaker placement. During ventricular systole, blood regurgitates into the right atrium, so the normal fall in atrial pressure (the x descent) is blunted or absent and the v wave is large. The regurgitant flow also produces systolic hepatic pulsation. Congestion of systemic veins explains the ascites-like distension and leg edema.

B.reason: A prominent y descent is seen in constrictive pericarditis, where early diastolic filling is rapid before the rigid pericardium halts expansion. This patient has a holosystolic murmur and a pulsatile liver instead.

C.reason: An absent y descent occurs in cardiac tamponade, in which ventricular filling is impeded by pericardial fluid. Her presentation is chronic and has a regurgitant murmur.

D.reason: Absent a waves occur in atrial fibrillation because atrial contraction is disorganized. Her rhythm is described as regular at 72/min, so this does not apply.

E.reason: Cannon a waves occur with AV dissociation when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve. She has a regular rate and no conduction block described.

high_yield_pearl: Tricuspid regurgitation: holosystolic murmur that rises with inspiration, with absent x descent and large v waves.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: TR is often due to RV dilatation and may be secondary to permanent pacemaker placement; infective endocarditis is another cause.
-  Clinical Findings: Holosystolic, high-pitched blowing murmur loudest at the tricuspid area; absent x descent on JVP; right-sided HF signs.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography with Doppler.
-  Management: Treat the underlying cause and right HF; surgical repair for severe disease.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with 20 minutes of palpitations and lightheadedness. Heart rate is 190/min, blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg, and the ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves. Vagal maneuvers fail, so a rapid bolus of adenosine is given, and the tachycardia terminates after a brief pause with transient flushing. Her heart rate returns to 88/min. Which of the following effects at the sinoatrial and AV nodal cells best explains this response?
option_A: Decreased slope of phase 4 spontaneous diastolic depolarization
option_B: Decreased slope of phase 0 by blockade of fast Na+ channels
option_D: Blockade of phase 3 delayed-rectifier K+ channels
correct_explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates after adenosine is consistent with an AV nodal reentrant PSVT. SA and AV nodal cells lack fast Na+ channels and depolarize slowly. Their phase 4 is a slow spontaneous diastolic depolarization caused by the funny current (If) through HCN channels, and the slope of phase 4 determines heart rate. Acetylcholine and adenosine decrease the rate of diastolic depolarization and thereby decrease heart rate, and in the AV node they briefly slow conduction enough to interrupt the reentrant circuit. Catecholamines do the opposite by increasing the slope and the chance that HCN channels are open.

B.reason: Nodal cells have no fast Na+ channels because these are permanently inactivated at their less negative resting potential, and phase 0 depends on Ca2+ channels. Class I antiarrhythmics block fast Na+ channels in ventricular and atrial myocytes and would not be effective here.

C.reason: A plateau (phase 2) exists in ventricular myocytes but is absent in the SA and AV nodes. Therefore prolongation of the plateau cannot be the mechanism of the response.

D.reason: Blockade of delayed-rectifier K+ channels prolongs repolarization and the QT interval, as with class III antiarrhythmics. It would not terminate this tachycardia and would not explain the brief pause.

E.reason: Increased opening of HCN channels increases the funny current and heart rate, which is the effect of sympathetic stimulation. Adenosine does the opposite.

high_yield_pearl: Adenosine and ACh slow the SA node by flattening the phase 4 slope (decreased If).
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Pacemaker action potential occurs in the SA and AV nodes; phase 4 is slow spontaneous diastolic depolarization from If (HCN channels); phase 0 is Ca2+ channel opening; phases 1 and 2 are absent.
-  Clinical Findings: Slope of phase 4 sets heart rate; ACh and adenosine lower it; catecholamines raise it.
-  Diagnostics: ECG.
-  Management: Adenosine terminates AV nodal reentrant SVT.

concept_name: Electrocardiogram: conduction pathway and AV node delay
stem: A 72-year-old woman has two episodes of syncope over 1 week. Heart rate is 52/min and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. ECG shows a regular rhythm with a P wave before every QRS complex, a PR interval of 320 msec, and a QRS duration of 88 msec. Cardiac catheterization is not needed, and the cardiologist notes that the conduction delay normally imposed at one site is about 100 msec. Which of the following structures is the usual source of this delay?
option_A: AV node
correct_explanation: A one-to-one P:QRS relationship with a prolonged PR interval of 320 msec (normal 120–200 msec) is first-degree AV block, and the narrow QRS places the delay above the His-Purkinje system. The AV node normally imposes a 100-msec delay that allows time for ventricular filling. This delay arises because AV nodal conduction is slow, since the cells depend on Ca2+ channels and lack fast Na+ channels. Speed of conduction is fastest in the His-Purkinje system, then atria, then ventricles, and slowest in the AV node. The AV node receives its blood supply through the PDA, so inferior ischemia or degenerative disease can lengthen the PR interval.

B.reason: The bundle of His is part of the rapidly conducting His-Purkinje system, which has the fastest conduction. A His lesion would more commonly widen the QRS than lengthen the PR in isolation.

C.reason: Purkinje fibers conduct rapidly and distribute the impulse to the ventricles. A narrow QRS argues against disease in this region.

D.reason: Bachmann bundle carries impulses from the right to the left atrium and affects interatrial conduction, not AV conduction. It is not the source of the physiologic 100-msec delay.

E.reason: The SA node is the dominant pacemaker that generates P waves. This patient has a P wave before each QRS, so the SA node is working and the delay lies after atrial depolarization.

high_yield_pearl: The AV node supplies the 100-msec delay (PR interval) and is perfused by the PDA.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Conduction runs SA node to atria (Bachmann bundle) to AV node to His to bundle branches to Purkinje fibers. The AV node delay of 100 msec allows ventricular filling; its blood supply is via the PDA. Conduction speed: His-Purkinje > atria > ventricles > AV node.
-  Clinical Findings: PR interval 120–200 msec; QRS under 100 msec; P wave is atrial depolarization.
-  Diagnostics: ECG.
-  Management: First-degree AV block needs no treatment.

stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after a motorcycle collision with head trauma. His blood pressure is 196/104 mm Hg, heart rate is 46/min, and respirations are slow and irregular. Pupils are unequal, and CT shows an expanding epidural hematoma with midline shift. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his bradycardia?
option_A: Peripheral baroreceptor activation by hypertension increasing vagal outflow
option_B: Decreased aortic baroreceptor firing from hypotension
option_D: Direct sympathetic suppression by cerebral hypoxia
correct_explanation: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations form Cushing triad, and the expanding hematoma indicates raised intracranial pressure. Increased pressure constricts cerebral arterioles and causes cerebral ischemia, which raises PCO2 and lowers pH. This triggers a central reflex sympathetic surge that increases perfusion pressure, producing hypertension. The elevated arterial pressure stretches the aortic arch and carotid sinus baroreceptors, which increase afferent firing to the nucleus tractus solitarius. The medulla then raises parasympathetic (vagal) output and lowers sympathetic output to the heart, causing the reflex bradycardia.

B.reason: Decreased baroreceptor firing occurs with hypotension, as in hypovolemic shock, and causes tachycardia and vasoconstriction. This patient is hypertensive, so baroreceptor firing is increased.

C.reason: Peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated by low PO2, high PCO2, or low pH and mainly drive respiration and sympathetic tone. They do not account for the bradycardia in this reflex.

D.reason: Cerebral ischemia causes a central sympathetic surge, not suppression, and the surge explains the hypertension. Sympathetic suppression would lower blood pressure.

E.reason: Central chemoreceptors become less sensitive with chronically elevated PCO2, such as in COPD. This is not relevant to an acute head injury, and it would not produce bradycardia.

high_yield_pearl: Cushing reflex: high ICP leads to hypertension, then baroreceptor-mediated bradycardia and respiratory depression.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Baroreceptors (aortic arch via CN X, carotid sinus via CN IX) project to the nucleus tractus solitarius. Cushing reflex: increased ICP leads to cerebral ischemia with increased PCO2 and decreased pH, central sympathetic surge and hypertension, then baroreceptor-induced bradycardia.
-  Clinical Findings: Hypertension, bradycardia, respiratory depression.
-  Diagnostics: CT head for the cause of increased ICP.
-  Management: Reduce ICP and treat the underlying lesion.

concept_name: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with 5 days of periorbital swelling that has progressed to pitting ankle edema. Blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg and heart rate is 88/min. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein without blood, and serum albumin is 1.7 g/dL. Jugular veins are flat, and there are no signs of heart failure. Which of the following changes in Starling forces is the primary cause of his edema?
option_A: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure
correct_explanation: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and periorbital edema in a child indicate nephrotic syndrome. Net fluid flow across capillaries follows Jv = Kf [(Pc - Pi) - sigma(pi c - pi i)]. Plasma oncotic pressure (pi c) pulls fluid into the capillary, so when albumin is lost in urine, pi c falls and net outward filtration increases. Fluid accumulates in the interstitium, producing edema that is first apparent in loose tissue such as the periorbital area. Flat neck veins and no cardiac findings argue against increased hydrostatic pressure, as in heart failure.

B.reason: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) causes edema in heart failure or venous obstruction. This patient has flat neck veins and no cardiac disease, so his hydrostatic pressure is not raised.

C.reason: Increased capillary permeability (Kf) occurs with toxins, infections, and burns, which are not present in this patient. His edema is explained by the measured albumin loss.

D.reason: Increased interstitial oncotic pressure occurs with lymphatic blockage, which traps proteins in the interstitium. This patient has no lymphatic obstruction, and he loses protein in urine rather than retaining it in tissue.

E.reason: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the capillary, so a decrease would increase outward filtration, but this is not a recognized cause of his disease. The hypoalbuminemia, not tissue pressure, is the primary abnormality.

high_yield_pearl: Nephrotic syndrome causes edema by lowering plasma oncotic pressure.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Jv = Kf[(Pc - Pi) - sigma(pi c - pi i)]. Edema is caused by increased Pc (HF), increased Kf (toxins, infection, burns), increased pi i (lymphatic blockage), or decreased pi c (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure, protein malnutrition).
-  Clinical Findings: Pitting edema; periorbital edema in nephrotic syndrome.
-  Diagnostics: Urine protein, serum albumin.
-  Management: Treat the cause; diuretics for symptoms.

stem: A 14-month-old boy has episodes of deep blue discoloration and irritability after crying, and he often squats during play. His mother notes failure to thrive, and his oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. A harsh systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border with a single S2. Chest radiograph shows a boot-shaped heart with decreased pulmonary vascular markings. Squatting improves his cyanosis by which of the following mechanisms?
option_A: Increased systemic vascular resistance, decreasing right-to-left shunting
option_D: Closure of the patent ductus arteriosus
option_E: Relief of the VSD by compression of the ventricular septum
correct_explanation: Cyanotic spells with crying, squatting, a boot-shaped heart, and reduced pulmonary vascular markings indicate tetralogy of Fallot. It results from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, producing pulmonary infundibular stenosis, RVH, an overriding aorta, and a VSD. The stenosis forces right-to-left flow across the VSD, and tet spells follow crying, fever, or exercise that worsens the right ventricular outflow obstruction. Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, which raises left ventricular pressure relative to right ventricular pressure. This decreases right-to-left shunting across the VSD and improves pulmonary blood flow and oxygenation. Pulmonary infundibular stenosis is the most important determinant of prognosis.

B.reason: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance would increase right-to-left shunting and worsen cyanosis. Squatting does not raise pulmonary resistance.

C.reason: Decreased systemic vascular resistance would favor right-to-left flow across the VSD and worsen cyanosis. Squatting does the opposite.

D.reason: The ductus arteriosus is not the mechanism of benefit in tetralogy, and ductal closure would reduce pulmonary blood flow in ductal-dependent lesions. Squatting acts on systemic resistance within seconds.

E.reason: Squatting does not mechanically close the VSD. The improvement is hemodynamic, resulting from a change in the pressure balance across the defect.

high_yield_pearl: In tetralogy of Fallot, squatting raises SVR and cuts the right-to-left shunt.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum gives pulmonary infundibular stenosis, RVH, overriding aorta, and VSD (PROVe). Associated with 22q11 syndromes.
-  Clinical Findings: Most common cause of early childhood cyanosis; tet spells with crying, fever, or exercise; boot-shaped heart.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography; chest radiograph.
-  Management: Squatting increases SVR, decreases right-to-left shunt; surgical repair.

stem: A 24-year-old woman was told as a child that she had a ventricular septal defect, but she was lost to follow-up. She now has exertional dyspnea, bluish discoloration of the lips and toes, and clubbing of the fingers and toes. Hematocrit is 62%, and examination shows a loud P2 with a right ventricular heave. Echocardiography shows a large VSD with right-to-left shunting and right ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following best explains the reversal of her shunt?
option_A: Pulmonary vascular remodeling with pulmonary arterial hypertension and RV pressure exceeding LV pressure
option_E: Increased systemic vascular resistance from hypertension
correct_explanation: An uncorrected left-to-right shunt with late cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia defines Eisenmenger syndrome. Chronic left-to-right flow increases pulmonary blood flow, which causes pathologic remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature and pulmonary arterial hypertension. The right ventricle hypertrophies to compensate, and a loud P2 and RV heave reflect high pulmonary pressure. When right ventricular pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure, the shunt reverses to right-to-left, delivering deoxygenated blood to the systemic circulation. Chronic hypoxemia causes secondary polycythemia and clubbing.

B.reason: Infundibular pulmonary stenosis is part of tetralogy of Fallot and presents with cyanosis in early childhood. This patient was acyanotic for years and has a loud P2, which indicates pulmonary hypertension, not outflow obstruction.

C.reason: PDA is a separate left-to-right shunt that causes differential cyanosis when it reverses. The echocardiogram shows the right-to-left flow at the VSD.

D.reason: Left ventricular failure would raise left-sided pressures and increase left-to-right shunting, not reverse it. Right-sided pressure must exceed left-sided pressure for reversal.

E.reason: Increased systemic resistance would favor left-to-right flow and would not produce cyanosis. Reversal requires a rise in pulmonary pressure.

high_yield_pearl: Eisenmenger: untreated left-to-right shunt leads to pulmonary hypertension, shunt reversal, cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Uncorrected left-to-right shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA) increases pulmonary blood flow, causing pulmonary vascular remodeling and pulmonary arterial hypertension; RVH occurs and the shunt becomes right-to-left when RV pressure exceeds LV pressure.
-  Clinical Findings: Late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography; right heart catheterization.
-  Management: Prevent by early closure of significant shunts.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for headaches and leg cramps with exertion. She is 142 cm tall and has primary amenorrhea and a webbed neck. Blood pressure is 164/102 mm Hg in the right arm and 104/72 mm Hg in the leg, and femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with the radial pulses. Chest radiograph shows notching of the inferior ribs. Which of the following additional cardiac abnormalities is she most likely to have?
option_A: Bicuspid aortic valve
correct_explanation: Short stature, primary amenorrhea, and a webbed neck suggest Turner syndrome, and hypertension in the arms with weak delayed femoral pulses and rib notching defines coarctation of the aorta. The narrowing is typically juxtaductal, near the insertion of the ductus arteriosus, so upper extremity blood pressure is higher than lower extremity pressure. Collateral flow through enlarged intercostal arteries erodes the ribs over time and produces rib notching on x-ray. Coarctation is associated with bicuspid aortic valve, other heart defects, and Turner syndrome. Complications include heart failure, berry aneurysm hemorrhage, aortic rupture, and infective endocarditis.

B.reason: Ebstein anomaly is associated with in utero lithium exposure and causes tricuspid regurgitation and accessory pathways. It is not associated with Turner syndrome or coarctation.

C.reason: Secundum ASD is the most common ASD and is associated with Down syndrome. It causes fixed S2 splitting, which is not described here, and is not a feature of Turner syndrome.

D.reason: Supravalvular aortic stenosis is associated with Williams syndrome, which has elfin facies and hypercalcemia. This patient's webbed neck and amenorrhea indicate Turner syndrome.

E.reason: D-transposition of the great arteries causes severe cyanosis in the first days of life and is associated with maternal diabetes. This patient is acyanotic and survived to adolescence.

high_yield_pearl: Turner syndrome: bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Aortic narrowing near the insertion of the ductus arteriosus (juxtaductal). Associated with bicuspid aortic valve, other heart defects, and Turner syndrome.
-  Clinical Findings: Upper extremity hypertension; weak, delayed lower-extremity pulses (brachiofemoral delay); rib notching with age.
-  Diagnostics: BP in all limbs; chest radiograph; echocardiography or CT.
-  Management: Surgical or catheter repair; complications include HF, cerebral hemorrhage (berry aneurysm), aortic rupture, and infective endocarditis.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a 35-pack-year smoking history, hypertension, and an LDL cholesterol of 182 mg/dL dies suddenly. Autopsy shows a left anterior descending artery with an eccentric fibrous plaque in the tunica intima. Histology shows a lipid-rich core containing foam cells, with a cap of smooth muscle cells and extracellular matrix. Smooth muscle cells from the media have migrated into the intima. Which of the following growth factors are most directly involved in this migration and proliferation?
option_A: Platelet-derived growth factor and fibroblast growth factor
correct_explanation: A lipid core with foam cells and a smooth muscle and matrix cap in a smoker with hypercholesterolemia represents a fibrous plaque of atherosclerosis in the coronary artery. Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial cell dysfunction, followed by macrophage and LDL accumulation and foam cell formation, producing fatty streaks. Smooth muscle cells then migrate from the media into the intima, a process involving PDGF and FGF, and they proliferate and deposit extracellular matrix to form the fibrous plaque. Complex atheromas can then calcify, and calcium content correlates with the risk of complications. The abdominal aorta is the most common location, followed by the coronary, popliteal, carotid, and circle of Willis arteries.

B.reason: VEGF promotes angiogenesis and endothelial proliferation and is not the factor listed for smooth muscle migration in plaque formation. The histology shows smooth muscle cells in the intima, not new vessel growth.

C.reason: EGF acts on epithelial and some mesenchymal cells and is not cited in First Aid as a driver of plaque smooth muscle migration. The relevant mediators are PDGF and FGF.

D.reason: Nerve growth factor supports neuronal survival and has no role in the intimal smooth muscle migration of atherosclerosis.

E.reason: Insulin-like growth factor binding protein modulates IGF signaling and is not described as a mediator of plaque smooth muscle cell migration. The plaque histology is explained by PDGF and FGF.

high_yield_pearl: Plaque smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima under PDGF and FGF.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Cholesterol plaque deposition in the tunica intima of elastic and large or medium muscular arteries. Sequence: endothelial dysfunction, macrophage and LDL accumulation, foam cells, fatty streaks, smooth muscle migration (PDGF, FGF), fibrous plaque, complex atheroma, calcification.
-  Clinical Findings: Angina, claudication, or asymptomatic. Location: abdominal aorta > coronary > popliteal > carotid > circle of Willis.
-  Diagnostics: Lipid panel; imaging as indicated.
-  Management: Statins lower LDL and reduce plaque progression and rupture risk; modify hypertension, smoking, diabetes.

stem: A 69-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with sudden severe abdominal and back pain. Blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg and heart rate is 128/min, and a tender pulsatile abdominal mass is palpated. Bedside ultrasonography shows a 7.2-cm infrarenal aortic aneurysm with retroperitoneal fluid. He is taken emergently to the operating room, where the surgeon explains why aneurysms favor this particular segment. Which of the following best explains the infrarenal predilection?
option_A: Reduced distribution of vasa vasorum in the infrarenal aorta
option_B: Cystic medial degeneration from a connective tissue disorder
option_C: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum from tertiary syphilis
option_D: Smooth muscle proliferation with onion skinning of arterioles
option_E: Leak of plasma proteins into the subendothelium
correct_explanation: Hypotension, a pulsatile abdominal mass, and acute abdominal and back pain form the classic triad of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Abdominal aortic aneurysm is associated with transmural inflammation and extracellular matrix degradation, and tobacco smoking is the strongest risk factor, along with age, male sex, and family history. Most aneurysms are infrarenal because the distribution of the vasa vasorum is reduced in this segment, leaving the wall relatively poorly nourished and prone to degeneration. Weakening of the wall leads to progressive dilation, and rupture presents with the triad described. Thoracic aneurysms, by contrast, are associated with cystic medial degeneration and tertiary syphilis.

B.reason: Cystic medial degeneration is associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms, such as in Marfan syndrome and with bicuspid aortic valve. This patient has an infrarenal abdominal aneurysm driven by smoking and atherosclerotic inflammation.

C.reason: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in tertiary syphilis affects the thoracic aorta and can dilate the aortic root. It does not explain an infrarenal abdominal aneurysm in a smoker.

D.reason: Onion skinning is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis from severe hypertension, which affects small arteries and arterioles. It does not cause a large focal dilation of the aorta.

E.reason: Plasma protein leak into the subendothelium describes hyaline arteriolosclerosis in hypertension or diabetes. It affects small vessels and does not produce an aortic aneurysm.

high_yield_pearl: Ruptured AAA: pulsatile abdominal mass, abdominal/back pain, and hypotension in a smoker.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Localized pathologic dilation of the aorta; AAA has transmural inflammation and matrix degradation; most often infrarenal (reduced vasa vasorum). Smoking is the strongest risk factor; age, male sex, and family history also contribute.
-  Clinical Findings: Palpable pulsatile abdominal mass; pain suggests leak, dissection, or imminent rupture; rupture triad of mass, abdominal or back pain, and resistant hypotension.
-  Diagnostics: Ultrasonography, CT.
-  Management: Surgical or endovascular repair; emergent repair for rupture.

stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing untreated hypertension presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. Blood pressure is 178/98 mm Hg in the right arm and 126/70 mm Hg in the left arm, and an early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum, and CT angiography shows an intimal flap beginning at the aortic root and extending into the arch. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management?
option_A: Emergent surgical repair
option_B: Intravenous beta-blocker followed by vasodilators alone
option_E: Oral calcium channel blocker with outpatient follow-up
correct_explanation: Tearing chest pain radiating to the back, unequal arm blood pressures, and a widened mediastinum point to aortic dissection, and hypertension is the strongest risk factor. The CT shows involvement of the ascending aorta, which is Stanford type A. A type A dissection can cause acute aortic regurgitation, as in the diastolic murmur here, and can cause cardiac tamponade or rupture. Because of these risks, type A dissection is treated with emergent surgery. Type B dissection, which involves only the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, is managed with beta-blockers followed by vasodilators.

B.reason: Beta-blockers followed by vasodilators is the treatment of Stanford type B dissection. This patient has ascending aortic involvement, and medical therapy alone would leave him at risk of rupture, tamponade, and worsening regurgitation.

C.reason: Fibrinolysis is considered in STEMI when primary PCI is unavailable and would be catastrophic in aortic dissection by causing bleeding into the false lumen. His presentation is not an acute coronary occlusion.

D.reason: Heparin is used in unstable angina and NSTEMI to prevent thrombus propagation. In dissection, anticoagulation would promote hemorrhage and extension of the false lumen.

E.reason: A calcium channel blocker alone does not control the shear forces on the aortic wall and is not appropriate for an acute type A dissection. Outpatient follow-up would be dangerous given the risk of rupture.

high_yield_pearl: Stanford A dissection (ascending aorta) needs surgery; type B gets beta-blockers then vasodilators.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Longitudinal intimal tear forming a false lumen; hypertension is the strongest risk factor; also bicuspid aortic valve and connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome).
-  Clinical Findings: Tearing, sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the back; unequal arm BPs; mediastinal widening.
-  Diagnostics: CT angiography; chest radiograph.
-  Management: Type A (ascending): surgery. Type B (below the left subclavian): beta-blockers, then vasodilators. Complications: organ ischemia, embolic stroke, rupture, acute AR, tamponade.

stem: A 44-year-old woman who smokes and takes sumatriptan for migraines has episodes of crushing chest pain that wake her from sleep in the early morning. During one episode, ECG shows transient ST elevation in the inferior leads that resolves within minutes after sublingual nitroglycerin. Troponin is normal, and coronary angiography shows no fixed obstructive disease. She has no exertional symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
option_A: Calcium channel blocker, nitrates, and smoking cessation
option_D: Percutaneous coronary intervention with stent placement
correct_explanation: Rest chest pain with transient ST elevation, a normal troponin, and normal coronary arteries on angiography define vasospastic angina, formerly Prinzmetal or variant angina. It results from coronary artery spasm rather than a fixed atherosclerotic lesion, so there is no infarction. Tobacco smoking is a major risk factor, and triggers include cocaine, amphetamines, alcohol, and triptans, which this patient uses. Treatment consists of calcium channel blockers and nitrates to relieve the spasm and smoking cessation. Drugs that provoke vasospasm should be avoided.

B.reason: Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker that can exacerbate vasospasm in vasospastic angina through unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction. It is therefore avoided in this condition.

C.reason: Fibrinolysis treats an occlusive thrombus in STEMI. This patient has transient ST elevation that resolved with nitroglycerin and normal arteries, so there is no thrombus to lyse.

D.reason: A stent treats a fixed obstructive lesion, and angiography shows none. The patient's symptoms arise from spasm, which a stent would not prevent.

E.reason: Dual antiplatelet therapy is part of treatment for unstable angina and NSTEMI. Her troponin is normal, there is no plaque rupture, and her ST elevation was transient with spasm.

high_yield_pearl: Rest angina with transient ST elevation and normal coronaries means vasospasm: treat with CCBs and nitrates.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Chest pain due to ischemic myocardium secondary to coronary narrowing or spasm, with no necrosis. Vasospastic angina occurs at rest due to coronary spasm; smoking is a major risk factor; triggers include cocaine, amphetamines, alcohol, triptans.
-  Clinical Findings: Rest pain; transient ischemic ST changes.
-  Diagnostics: ECG during episodes; normal biomarkers.
-  Management: Calcium channel blockers, nitrates, smoking cessation.

stem: A 66-year-old man with diabetes and known 80% proximal stenosis of the left anterior descending artery undergoes a pharmacologic stress test because he cannot exercise. Within minutes of regadenoson infusion, he develops substernal chest pressure and ST depression in the anterior leads. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and heart rate is 92/min. Symptoms resolve after the test is stopped and aminophylline is given. Which of the following best explains the ischemia during this test?
option_A: Dilation of normal coronary vessels diverting blood away from maximally dilated stenosed vessels
option_B: Coronary artery spasm in a vessel with normal architecture
option_C: Acute rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with thrombosis
option_E: Transient post-ischemic dysfunction of viable myocardium
correct_explanation: Vessels distal to a coronary stenosis are maximally dilated at baseline to compensate for the reduced flow. Vasodilators such as dipyridamole, adenosine, and regadenoson dilate the normal vessels, which lowers resistance and hydrostatic pressure in the healthy coronary arteries. Blood is therefore shunted toward the well-perfused territories and flow falls to the myocardium supplied by the stenosed vessel, causing ischemia, which is called coronary steal. Vasodilator stress tests rely on this differential flow to detect ischemia, and rarely they cause true ischemia as seen here. The ischemia resolves when the vasodilator effect is reversed.

B.reason: Vasospastic angina results from coronary spasm and typically occurs at rest in a patient with minimal fixed disease. This patient has a known fixed stenosis, and his symptoms began right after a vasodilator was infused.

C.reason: Plaque rupture with thrombosis causes acute coronary syndrome, with ongoing pain and biomarker elevation. His symptoms resolved quickly once the vasodilator was reversed, which argues against thrombosis.

D.reason: Increased preload would raise wall tension and oxygen demand, but regadenoson is a vasodilator that lowers pressure in normal vessels. The mechanism described is a redistribution of flow, not a rise in preload.

E.reason: Myocardial stunning is transient, reversible LV systolic dysfunction after a brief, acute ischemic episode. It is a consequence of ischemia, not the explanation for what triggered it in this setting.

high_yield_pearl: Vasodilation of healthy vessels steals blood from stenosed vessels.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Distal to a coronary stenosis, vessels are maximally dilated; vasodilators (dipyridamole, adenosine, regadenoson) dilate normal vessels, decrease their pressure, and shunt blood away from the stenosed territory.
-  Clinical Findings: Chest pain and ST changes during vasodilator stress testing.
-  Diagnostics: Vasodilator stress tests rely on differential flow.
-  Management: Stop the vasodilator; reversal with aminophylline.

stem: A 62-year-old man is hospitalized with an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI. On hospital day 2, he develops sharp, pleuritic chest pain that improves when he leans forward. Temperature is 37.9°C and a scratchy three-component sound is heard along the left sternal border. Troponin is declining, and he remains hemodynamically stable. Which of the following microscopic findings in the infarcted myocardium would be expected at this time?
option_A: Extensive coagulative necrosis with neutrophilic infiltrate
option_C: Macrophages and granulation tissue at the margins
option_E: Hypercontraction of myofibrils with dark eosinophilic stripes only
correct_explanation: Pleuritic, positional chest pain with a friction rub 2 days after an MI is postinfarction fibrinous pericarditis. At 1–3 days, the infarct shows extensive coagulative necrosis, and the tissue surrounding the infarct shows acute inflammation with neutrophils. The inflamed necrotic myocardium irritates the overlying epicardium and causes fibrinous pericarditis, which is usually self-limited. The sequence progresses to macrophages and granulation tissue at 3–14 days and a contracted scar after 2 weeks to several months. Grossly the infarct at this stage shows central yellow-brown softening with a hyperemic border.

B.reason: Wavy fibers are seen in the first 0–4 hours, before neutrophils arrive. This patient is on hospital day 2, well past the earliest changes.

C.reason: Macrophages and granulation tissue at the margins appear at 3–14 days, the window for free wall, papillary muscle, and septal rupture. He is only on day 2.

D.reason: A contracted scar is complete at 2 weeks to several months and is associated with Dressler syndrome, heart failure, and true aneurysm. It cannot be present after 2 days.

E.reason: Hypercontraction of myofibrils is a feature of reperfusion injury seen in the first 24 hours. By day 2 neutrophils and extensive coagulative necrosis dominate the histology.

high_yield_pearl: Day 1–3 MI: neutrophils and fibrinous pericarditis; day 3–14: macrophages and rupture risk.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: MI evolution: 0–24 h wavy fibers then early coagulative necrosis (reperfusion injury possible); 1–3 days extensive necrosis with neutrophils; 3–14 days macrophages then granulation tissue; 2 weeks to months contracted scar.
-  Clinical Findings: Day 1–3: postinfarction fibrinous pericarditis; day 3–14: free wall, papillary, and septal rupture, pseudoaneurysm; later: Dressler syndrome, HF, true aneurysm.
-  Diagnostics: ECG, troponin; tetrazolium stain on gross specimens.
-  Management: Reperfusion; treat complications.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with diabetes presents with 90 minutes of chest pressure and dyspnea. Blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg and heart rate is 84/min. ECG shows ST elevation in leads I and aVL with reciprocal ST depression in leads II, III, and aVF, and troponin is elevated. She is taken for primary PCI. Which of the following arteries is most likely the culprit?
option_A: Left circumflex artery
correct_explanation: ST elevation in leads I and aVL with reciprocal depression in the inferior leads localizes a lateral infarct. Lateral infarction corresponds to the left circumflex artery. Different territories produce ST changes in different leads: anteroseptal (LAD) in V1–V2, anteroapical (distal LAD) in V3–V4, anterolateral (LAD or LCX) in V5–V6, inferior (RCA or LCX) in II, III, and aVF, and posterior (PDA) in V7–V9 with ST depression in V1–V3 and tall R waves. The elevated troponin and persistent ST elevation confirm a STEMI requiring reperfusion.

B.reason: A proximal LAD occlusion produces anteroseptal changes in V1–V2 and often more extensive anterior ST elevation. This patient's ST elevation is limited to I and aVL.

C.reason: A distal LAD occlusion produces anteroapical changes in V3–V4. The leads involved here are lateral, not precordial.

D.reason: An RCA occlusion produces inferior ST elevation in II, III, and aVF, and in this patient those leads show reciprocal ST depression. The pattern is opposite to that of an inferior STEMI.

E.reason: A PDA occlusion produces posterior infarction, seen as ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves and ST elevation in V7–V9. This patient's ST elevation is in I and aVL.

high_yield_pearl: Lateral STEMI (I, aVL) points to the LCX.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Occlusion of a coronary artery causes transmural infarction in its territory.
-  Clinical Findings: Anteroseptal (LAD): V1–V2; anteroapical (distal LAD): V3–V4; anterolateral (LAD or LCX): V5–V6; lateral (LCX): I, aVL; inferior (RCA or LCX): II, III, aVF; posterior (PDA): V7–V9 with ST depression in V1–V3.
-  Diagnostics: ECG is the gold standard in the first 6 hours; troponin I rises after 4 hours.
-  Management: Reperfusion, preferably PCI.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with palpitations and lightheadedness. He has a prior ECG with a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS. Blood pressure is 106/64 mm Hg and heart rate is 220/min with an irregularly irregular, wide-complex rhythm. He is awake and alert and has no chest pain. Which of the following medications should be avoided in this patient?
option_A: Verapamil
option_E: Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway
correct_explanation: A short PR interval with a delta wave and a wide-complex irregular tachycardia at 220/min indicate atrial fibrillation conducted over the bundle of Kent in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. The accessory pathway bypasses the rate-slowing AV node, so the ventricles are partially depolarized earlier, and rapid atrial impulses are conducted directly to the ventricles. AV nodal-blocking drugs such as adenosine, calcium channel blockers, and beta-blockers block the normal pathway and favor conduction over the accessory pathway, which can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. The recommended drugs for treatment are procainamide and ibutilide. Verapamil is therefore contraindicated.

B.reason: Procainamide is a first-line treatment for WPW with atrial fibrillation because it slows conduction over the accessory pathway. It is therefore appropriate rather than avoided.

C.reason: Ibutilide is also recommended for WPW arrhythmias. It prolongs repolarization and does not preferentially favor accessory pathway conduction.

D.reason: Synchronized cardioversion is appropriate if a patient becomes unstable and is part of rhythm control for atrial fibrillation. It does not block the AV node pharmacologically.

E.reason: Catheter ablation is the definitive therapy for symptomatic WPW and SVT because it eliminates the reentry circuit. It is a safe, standard treatment.

high_yield_pearl: WPW with AF: avoid AV nodal blockers; use procainamide or ibutilide.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Abnormal fast accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) from atria to ventricle bypasses the AV node; ventricles partially depolarize earlier, which can create a reentry circuit and SVT.
-  Clinical Findings: Delta wave, wide QRS, short PR interval.
-  Diagnostics: ECG.
-  Management: Procainamide, ibutilide; avoid AV nodal-blocking drugs (adenosine, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers); catheter ablation for definitive therapy.

concept_name: Torsades de pointes and drug-induced long QT
stem: A 34-year-old woman with schizophrenia is brought in after two episodes of syncope. Her medications include haloperidol and, for the past 3 days, ondansetron for gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea. Blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, and serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. Telemetry shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with shifting sinusoidal QRS axis, and the QTc on the baseline strip is 540 msec. She is awake and hemodynamically stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
option_A: Intravenous magnesium sulfate
correct_explanation: A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting QRS axis and a long QT interval is torsades de pointes. The long QT in this patient has multiple contributors: haloperidol, ondansetron, and hypokalemia from vomiting and diarrhea. Torsades can progress to ventricular fibrillation, so unstable patients need defibrillation, while stable patients are treated with magnesium sulfate. Electrolyte abnormalities such as low K+, low Mg2+, and low Ca2+ should be corrected, and the offending drugs stopped. Drugs that further prolong the QT interval must be avoided.

B.reason: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic that prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes. It is therefore inappropriate in this setting.

C.reason: Procainamide is a class IA agent that prolongs the action potential duration and QT interval. Giving it to a patient with torsades could worsen the arrhythmia.

D.reason: Lidocaine is a class IB drug used for ventricular arrhythmias after MI and digitalis toxicity. It is not the recommended therapy for torsades, where magnesium is used for stable patients.

E.reason: Adenosine terminates AV nodal reentrant SVT. This patient has a ventricular rhythm that does not depend on the AV node, so adenosine would be ineffective.

high_yield_pearl: Torsades: stable gets magnesium sulfate, unstable gets defibrillation; fix K+ and stop QT-prolonging drugs.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Polymorphic VT with shifting sinusoidal waveforms; long QT predisposes. Caused by drugs, low K+, low Mg2+, low Ca2+. Drug-induced long QT (ABCDEF+NO): antiarrhythmics (Ia, III), arsenic, antibiotics (macrolides, fluoroquinolones), antipsychotics (haloperidol), chloroquine, antidepressants (TCAs), diuretics (thiazides), antiemetics (ondansetron), antifungals (fluconazole), protease inhibitors (navirs), opioids (methadone).
-  Clinical Findings: Syncope, palpitations, risk of VF.
-  Diagnostics: ECG with QTc; electrolytes.
-  Management: Defibrillation if unstable; magnesium sulfate if stable.

concept_name: Conduction blocks: second-degree AV block (Mobitz type II)
stem: A 74-year-old man with prior anteroseptal MI has two syncopal episodes in 1 week. Heart rate is 46/min and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. ECG shows a constant PR interval of 180 msec with intermittent P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex, and the QRS duration is 140 msec. There is no progressive PR lengthening before the dropped beats. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
option_A: Permanent pacemaker
correct_explanation: Intermittent dropped QRS complexes without preceding PR prolongation, with a wide QRS, represent Mobitz type II second-degree AV block. This pattern usually indicates a structural abnormality in the conduction system below the AV node, such as ischemia or fibrosis, which fits his prior MI. It may progress to third-degree block, and in this patient it has already caused syncope. Treatment is usually a pacemaker. In contrast, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat, is usually asymptomatic, and requires no treatment.

B.reason: Observation is appropriate for first-degree block and for asymptomatic Mobitz type I. This patient has Mobitz type II with syncope and a wide QRS, so he needs definitive therapy.

C.reason: Atropine acts at the AV node and has only a short-term role in symptomatic bradycardia. It is not a long-term treatment and is unlikely to help infranodal block.

D.reason: Digoxin slows AV node conduction and would worsen block. It is used for heart failure and atrial fibrillation rate control.

E.reason: Adenosine transiently slows AV nodal conduction to terminate reentrant SVT. It would further impair conduction in a patient with AV block.

high_yield_pearl: Mobitz II: dropped beats without PR change; needs a pacemaker.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Mobitz II: dropped beats not preceded by a change in PR interval; usually indicates structural abnormality (ischemia, fibrosis); may progress to third-degree block.
-  Clinical Findings: Syncope or presyncope; bradycardia.
-  Diagnostics: ECG: constant PR with intermittent dropped QRS. Contrast with first-degree (PR above 200 msec) and Mobitz I (progressive PR lengthening).
-  Management: Usually a pacemaker; third-degree block also needs a pacemaker.

concept_name: Myocardial infarction complications: papillary muscle rupture
