stem: A 67-year-old man is hospitalized with an inferior STEMI. Four days later he develops sudden severe dyspnea and diaphoresis. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg and heart rate is 118/min. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex radiating to the axilla, and crackles fill both lung fields. Echocardiography shows a flail mitral leaflet with severe regurgitation and no pericardial effusion, and right-heart oxygen saturations are normal. Which structure has most likely ruptured, and why was it vulnerable?
option_A: Posteromedial papillary muscle, which has a single blood supply from the PDA
option_B: Anterolateral papillary muscle, which has a single supply from the LAD
option_C: Interventricular septum, which undergoes macrophage-mediated degradation
option_D: Left ventricular free wall, contained by adherent pericardium
option_E: Mitral annulus, which is weakened by rheumatic fever
correct_explanation: A new holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla with pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, and a flail mitral leaflet 2–7 days after an MI indicates papillary muscle rupture causing acute mitral regurgitation. The posteromedial papillary muscle ruptures far more often than the anterolateral muscle because it has a single blood supply from the posterior descending artery, whereas the anterolateral muscle has dual supply from the LAD and LCX. Her inferior infarct involves the PDA territory, so the posteromedial muscle undergoes necrosis. Normal right-heart saturations and no effusion exclude septal rupture and tamponade. The acute volume load on a non-dilated left atrium causes pulmonary edema.

B.reason: The anterolateral papillary muscle has a dual blood supply from the LAD and LCX, so it is much less vulnerable to rupture. Moreover, the patient's infarct is inferior, in the PDA territory.

C.reason: Interventricular septal rupture occurs at 3–5 days with macrophage-mediated degradation and causes a VSD, with a step-up in right-heart oxygen saturation and RV pressure. This patient has normal right-heart saturations and a flail mitral leaflet.

D.reason: Free wall rupture occurs at 5–14 days and causes tamponade or internal hemorrhage, often fatal. Echocardiography here shows no effusion, and the findings are those of mitral regurgitation.

E.reason: The mitral annulus is not involved in post-MI rupture, and rheumatic disease produces chronic valve disease rather than an acute flail leaflet. The timing and findings point to papillary muscle necrosis.

high_yield_pearl: Posteromedial papillary muscle has one blood supply (PDA), so it ruptures after inferior MI.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2–7 days post-MI; posteromedial much more than anterolateral because it has a single PDA supply, whereas the anterolateral has dual supply from LAD and LCX.
-  Clinical Findings: Acute mitral regurgitation, cardiogenic shock, severe pulmonary edema.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography showing flail leaflet; no step-up in right heart saturation.
-  Management: Hemodynamic support and surgical repair. Other MI complications: arrhythmia, pericarditis, septal rupture, pseudoaneurysm, free wall rupture, true aneurysm, Dressler syndrome.

stem: A 46-year-old man with a 20-year history of heavy alcohol use presents with 3 months of progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and ankle swelling. Blood pressure is 104/72 mm Hg and heart rate is 98/min, with jugular venous distention to 11 cm and an S3 at the apex. A soft holosystolic apical murmur is heard, and chest radiograph shows a globular, enlarged cardiac silhouette with pulmonary vascular congestion. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 22%. Which of the following best describes the pattern of myocardial remodeling in this condition?
option_A: Sarcomeres added in series (eccentric hypertrophy)
option_C: Myofibrillar disarray with fibrosis and asymmetric septal thickening
option_D: Eosinophilic infiltration of the endocardium and myocardium
option_E: Extracellular deposition of misfolded protein with a low-voltage ECG
correct_explanation: Heart failure with a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle, an S3, and functional mitral regurgitation in a heavy drinker indicates dilated cardiomyopathy, the most common cardiomyopathy (about 90% of cases). Etiologies include alcohol, cocaine, doxorubicin, Coxsackie B, Chagas disease, ischemia, and systemic conditions, and many cases are idiopathic or familial with TTN mutations that shorten titin. The loss of contractility produces systolic dysfunction and a volume-loaded ventricle that undergoes eccentric hypertrophy, in which sarcomeres are added in series. The dilated annulus causes the systolic regurgitant murmur, and the low ejection fraction causes the congestion. Treatment includes sodium restriction, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, beta-blockers, sacubitril-valsartan, diuretics, mineralocorticoid receptor blockers, an ICD, and transplantation.

B.reason: Concentric hypertrophy, with sarcomeres added in parallel, occurs with pressure overload and in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and produces a thick, small-cavity ventricle. This patient has a dilated cavity and a low ejection fraction.

C.reason: Myofibrillar disarray and fibrosis with septal hypertrophy describe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which causes exertional syncope and an S4, with outflow obstruction. This patient has a dilated ventricle with systolic failure.

D.reason: Eosinophilic infiltration is characteristic of Loffler endocarditis in the hypereosinophilic syndrome, a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. It would produce diastolic dysfunction with a non-dilated ventricle.

E.reason: Amyloid deposition causes restrictive cardiomyopathy with a low-voltage ECG despite thick myocardium. This patient has a dilated ventricle and no low-voltage pattern is described.

high_yield_pearl: Dilated cardiomyopathy gives eccentric hypertrophy with sarcomeres added in series and systolic failure.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Most common cardiomyopathy (90%); idiopathic or familial (TTN mutation); drugs (alcohol, cocaine, doxorubicin), infection (coxsackie B, Chagas), ischemia, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, thyrotoxicosis, wet beriberi, peripartum. Eccentric hypertrophy; systolic dysfunction.
-  Clinical Findings: HF, S3, systolic regurgitant murmur; balloon appearance on CXR.
-  Diagnostics: Dilated heart on echocardiogram.
-  Management: Na+ restriction, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers, sacubitril/valsartan, diuretics, MRAs, ICD, heart transplant.

concept_name: Heart failure: drug therapy and mortality benefit
stem: A 63-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 28% is evaluated in clinic for persistent dyspnea. He takes an ACE inhibitor, carvedilol, and spironolactone and has been stable for 3 months. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, jugular venous pressure is elevated, and he has bibasilar crackles and 2+ pitting edema to the knees. His physician plans to add a drug primarily to relieve congestion. Which of the following agents provides symptomatic relief in HFrEF but is not shown to reduce mortality?
option_A: Furosemide
correct_explanation: This patient has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction who remains congested despite foundational therapy. In HFrEF, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, beta-blockers (except in acute decompensated HF), and aldosterone receptor antagonists decrease mortality. Hydralazine with nitrate therapy and SGLT2 inhibitors decrease symptoms and mortality. Loop and thiazide diuretics are used mainly for symptomatic relief of congestion and do not have a proven mortality benefit. Furosemide is therefore the appropriate choice for this question.

B.reason: Spironolactone is an aldosterone receptor antagonist and reduces mortality in HFrEF. He already takes it, and it is not simply a symptomatic agent.

C.reason: Sacubitril-valsartan, an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, decreases mortality in HFrEF. It is combined with an ARB and cannot be given with an ACE inhibitor because of angioedema risk.

D.reason: Hydralazine with nitrate therapy decreases symptoms and mortality in HFrEF. It is therefore not the correct answer for a drug without mortality benefit.

E.reason: SGLT2 inhibitors decrease symptoms and mortality in HFrEF. They offer benefit beyond symptom relief and are not limited to decongestion.

high_yield_pearl: Loop diuretics relieve HF symptoms but do not improve survival.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: HFrEF: systolic dysfunction with increased EDV and decreased contractility; HFpEF: diastolic dysfunction with decreased compliance. Neurohormonal activation (catecholamines, angiotensin II, aldosterone, ADH) maintains BP and CO but causes deleterious remodeling.
-  Clinical Findings: Dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, S3, rales, JVD, pitting edema.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography; BNP.
-  Management: ACEi/ARBs, ARNI, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists decrease mortality in HFrEF; hydralazine with nitrates and SGLT2 inhibitors decrease symptoms and mortality; loop and thiazide diuretics for symptoms.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought in after a motor vehicle collision. Blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg and heart rate is 132/min, and her skin is cold and clammy. Her abdomen is distended and tender, and ultrasonography shows free fluid in the left upper quadrant. Right heart catheterization shows a central venous pressure of 1 mm Hg, a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 4 mm Hg, a low cardiac output, an elevated systemic vascular resistance, and a decreased mixed venous oxygen saturation. Which of the following types of shock does she have?
option_A: Hypovolemic shock
correct_explanation: A trauma patient with splenic injury and free abdominal fluid has hemorrhage causing volume depletion. The hemodynamic profile of hypovolemic shock is cold, clammy skin with low CVP, low PCWP, low cardiac output, high SVR from compensatory vasoconstriction, and low SvO2 from increased extraction. The tachycardia and cold skin reflect baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic activation. Cardiogenic shock would show high filling pressures, obstructive shock would show impeded filling, and distributive shock would show vasodilation with low SVR.

B.reason: Cardiogenic shock from left heart dysfunction raises CVP and PCWP because blood backs up behind the failing pump. This patient's pressures are low, and she has a clear source of volume loss.

C.reason: Cardiac tamponade is obstructive shock with impeded filling, elevated CVP, and often distant heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Her CVP is 1 mm Hg and there is no neck vein distention.

D.reason: Septic distributive shock produces warm, dry skin early, decreased SVR, and often fever. This patient has cold, clammy skin and elevated SVR.

E.reason: Distributive shock from CNS injury produces systemic vasodilation with decreased SVR. Her SVR is elevated and her skin is cold, which is opposite to this pattern.

high_yield_pearl: Hypovolemic shock: low CVP, low PCWP, low CO, high SVR, cold skin.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Shock is inadequate organ perfusion. Hypovolemic (hemorrhage, dehydration, burns): volume depletion. Cardiogenic (MI, HF, valvular, arrhythmia): left heart dysfunction. Obstructive (PE, tension pneumothorax, tamponade): impeded cardiopulmonary flow. Distributive (sepsis early, anaphylaxis, CNS injury): systemic vasodilation.
-  Clinical Findings: Hypovolemic: cold, clammy skin; low CVP, PCWP, CO, SvO2; high SVR. Distributive: warm, dry skin early.
-  Diagnostics: Hemodynamic profile.
-  Management: Treat the cause; restore volume in hypovolemia.

stem: A 67-year-old man has had 3 weeks of low-grade fevers, fatigue, and a 4-kg weight loss. Temperature is 38.1°C and heart rate is 92/min, and he has linear hemorrhages under several fingernails and painful violaceous nodules on his fingertips. A new diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on the aortic valve, and blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus in 3 of 3 bottles. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
option_A: Colonoscopy
correct_explanation: Subacute fever and weight loss with splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, a new regurgitant murmur, and a valvular vegetation indicate infective endocarditis. Splinter hemorrhages are a vascular phenomenon, and the painful violaceous fingertip nodules are Osler nodes, an immunologic phenomenon from immune complex deposition. Endothelial injury leads to vegetations of platelets, fibrin, and microbes. Infective endocarditis with Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S bovis) is associated with colon cancer, so colonoscopy is needed. Other associations include S epidermidis with prosthetic valves, Enterococcus with GI or GU procedures, and S aureus with injection drug use.

B.reason: Cystoscopy would be considered for a GU source, and Enterococcus is associated with GI or GU procedures. This patient's organism is S gallolyticus, which points to the colon.

C.reason: Dental procedures are a classic source of subacute endocarditis from viridans streptococci. This patient's organism is S gallolyticus, and dental extraction would not address the likely occult source.

D.reason: A bone marrow biopsy evaluates hematologic disease and is not part of the workup of culture-positive endocarditis. His cultures already identify the organism.

E.reason: A lumbar puncture would be considered for meningitis or CNS emboli with neurologic symptoms. This patient has no neurologic findings, and it would not identify the source of S gallolyticus bacteremia.

high_yield_pearl: S gallolyticus endocarditis means look for colon cancer.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Endothelial injury leads to vegetations of platelets, fibrin, and microbes; acute (S aureus, large vegetations on normal valves) vs subacute (viridans streptococci on abnormal valves). Associations: prosthetic valves, S epidermidis; GI/GU procedures, Enterococcus; colon cancer, S gallolyticus; HACEK; culture-negative: Coxiella, Bartonella; injection drug use: S aureus, Pseudomonas, Candida.
-  Clinical Findings: Fever, new murmur, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots; mitral valve most common, tricuspid in IVDU.
-  Diagnostics: Multiple blood cultures and echocardiography.
-  Management: Antibiotics; evaluate the source.

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents 3 weeks after a sore throat with fever, migratory pain and swelling in his knees and ankles, and a new apical holosystolic murmur. Examination shows firm, painless subcutaneous nodules over the elbows and an erythematous ring-shaped rash on the trunk. Anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers are elevated, and throat culture is now negative. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of his cardiac disease?
option_A: Antibodies to streptococcal M protein cross-reacting with myosin (type II hypersensitivity)
option_B: Direct bacterial invasion of the valve endothelium
option_C: Deposition of preformed immune complexes (type III hypersensitivity)
option_E: Cell-mediated destruction of cardiac myocytes by viral infection
correct_explanation: A latent period after pharyngitis followed by migratory polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, and erythema marginatum meets the J-N-E-S major criteria and indicates acute rheumatic fever. It is a nonsuppurative consequence of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis and is immune mediated, not due to direct bacterial effects. Antibodies to M protein cross-react with self antigens, often myosin, through molecular mimicry, a type II hypersensitivity reaction. The cardiac lesions include Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells, and the mitral valve is affected most, with early regurgitation and late stenosis. Penicillin is used for treatment and prophylaxis.

B.reason: Direct valve invasion causes infective endocarditis, which presents with fever, vegetations, and positive blood cultures. Rheumatic fever follows a negative throat culture and is not a direct effect of bacteria.

C.reason: Type III hypersensitivity involves immune complex deposition, as in postinfectious glomerulonephritis. First Aid classifies rheumatic fever as a type II hypersensitivity reaction with molecular mimicry.

D.reason: Superantigen-mediated cytokine release causes toxic shock syndrome with shock and a diffuse rash. This patient has polyarthritis and carditis after a latent period.

E.reason: Viral myocarditis is caused by direct infection, producing a lymphocytic infiltrate and sometimes heart failure. This patient has a streptococcal immune response with elevated ASO titers.

high_yield_pearl: Rheumatic fever is molecular mimicry between M protein and myosin: a type II hypersensitivity.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Nonsuppurative sequela of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis; type II hypersensitivity; M protein antibodies cross-react with myosin.
-  Clinical Findings: J-N-E-S: Joint (migratory polyarthritis), heart (pancarditis), Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea. Aschoff bodies, Anitschkow cells; mitral > aortic >> tricuspid; early regurgitation, late stenosis.
-  Diagnostics: Elevated ASO and anti-DNase B titers.
-  Management: Penicillin for treatment and prophylaxis.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of mediastinal radiation for lymphoma 15 years ago presents with progressive dyspnea, abdominal swelling, and leg edema. Blood pressure is 112/74 mm Hg and heart rate is 86/min, and the jugular venous pressure rises during inspiration. A high-pitched early diastolic sound is heard at the left sternal border, and CT shows a thickened, calcified pericardium. Which of the following best explains the inspiratory rise in his jugular venous pressure?
option_A: The right ventricle cannot accommodate the increased venous return, so blood backs up into the vena cava
option_B: Increased intrathoracic pressure impeding right atrial filling
option_C: Decreased right ventricular afterload during inspiration
correct_explanation: A history of mediastinal radiation, edema, a pericardial knock, and a calcified, thickened pericardium indicate constrictive pericarditis, in which fibrosis limits expansion of the heart. Normally, inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, increases venous return, and decreases the JVP. In constrictive pericarditis, impaired right ventricular filling means the RV cannot accommodate the increased venous return during inspiration. Blood backs up into the vena cava and the JVP rises paradoxically, which is Kussmaul sign. It is also seen with restrictive cardiomyopathy, right heart failure, massive pulmonary embolism, and right atrial or ventricular tumors.

B.reason: Inspiration decreases intrathoracic pressure, which augments venous return rather than impeding it. Increased intrathoracic pressure occurs during expiration or Valsalva.

C.reason: Right ventricular afterload does not explain the sign. The abnormality is in diastolic filling of a restricted ventricle, not in the outflow.

D.reason: Tricuspid regurgitation produces a prominent v wave and absent x descent but does not explain a paradoxical inspiratory rise in JVP. This patient has a pericardial knock and calcified pericardium.

E.reason: Reduced venous capacitance would raise the baseline JVP but would not produce a paradoxical rise specifically during inspiration. The mechanism here is restricted ventricular filling.

high_yield_pearl: Kussmaul sign: JVP rises on inspiration because the restricted RV cannot take the extra venous return.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Constrictive pericarditis: chronic inflammation leads to pericardial fibrosis and calcification, limiting ventricular filling; causes include idiopathic, viral, cardiac surgery, thoracic radiotherapy, and TB. Kussmaul sign: paradoxical JVP rise on inspiration due to impaired RV filling.
-  Clinical Findings: Dyspnea, edema, JVD, pericardial knock, Kussmaul sign; prominent y descent.
-  Diagnostics: CT or MRI showing thickened pericardium; echocardiography.
-  Management: Treat the cause; pericardiectomy for severe disease.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has 3 months of intermittent syncope when she stands up from a seated position, low-grade fevers, fatigue, and a 5-kg weight loss. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg and heart rate is 84/min, and an early diastolic low-pitched sound is heard at the apex that varies with position. ESR is 62 mm/h and hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL. Echocardiography shows a pedunculated, mobile mass in the left atrium attached to the interatrial septum. Which of the following mediators is most responsible for her constitutional symptoms?
option_A: Interleukin-6
correct_explanation: A mobile pedunculated left atrial mass with positional syncope, an early diastolic tumor plop, and constitutional symptoms indicates a cardiac myxoma, the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults. Ninety percent occur in the atria, mostly the left, where they produce intermittent ball-valve obstruction of the mitral orifice that causes syncope. The early diastolic tumor plop can mimic mitral stenosis. The tumor produces IL-6, which causes fever, weight loss, anemia, and an elevated ESR. Histology shows gelatinous material with myxoma cells in glycosaminoglycans.

B.reason: IL-2 stimulates T-cell proliferation and is not the cytokine linked to myxoma. The constitutional symptoms of myxoma are attributed to IL-6.

C.reason: Interferon-gamma activates macrophages and is not implicated in the systemic features of myxoma. The patient's findings are explained by tumor-derived IL-6.

D.reason: IL-4 promotes Th2 differentiation and IgE class switching and is unrelated to cardiac myxoma. It does not account for fever and weight loss here.

E.reason: TGF-beta promotes fibrosis and is not the mediator of myxoma-related constitutional symptoms. IL-6 is the recognized cytokine.

high_yield_pearl: Left atrial myxoma: ball-valve syncope, tumor plop, and IL-6-driven constitutional symptoms.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Most common primary cardiac tumor in adults; 90% in the atria (mostly left); IL-6 production causes constitutional symptoms. Most common cardiac tumor overall is metastasis (eg, melanoma). Rhabdomyoma is the most frequent primary tumor in children (tuberous sclerosis).
-  Clinical Findings: Ball-valve obstruction with syncope; fever, weight loss; early diastolic tumor plop.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography; histology shows gelatinous material with myxoma cells in glycosaminoglycans.
-  Management: Surgical resection.

stem: A 42-year-old man has 6 months of episodic pounding headaches, sweating, and palpitations. Blood pressure is 214/124 mm Hg and heart rate is 112/min, and plasma free metanephrines are markedly elevated. CT shows a 4-cm right adrenal mass, and he is scheduled for adrenalectomy. His physician plans to begin preoperative blood pressure control. Which of the following should be started first?
option_A: Phenoxybenzamine
correct_explanation: Paroxysmal headaches, diaphoresis, palpitations, severe hypertension, elevated metanephrines, and an adrenal mass indicate pheochromocytoma. Catecholamine excess stimulates both alpha and beta receptors. In pheochromocytoma, alpha-blockade with phentolamine or phenoxybenzamine must be started first, prior to resection, and beta-blockade is added afterward. Giving a beta-blocker first would block vasodilatory beta-2 receptors and leave alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can trigger a hypertensive crisis. Alpha-blockade first therefore ensures safe control of blood pressure.

B.reason: Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker, and starting it first leaves unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, which could precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Beta-blockade is added only after alpha-blockade.

C.reason: Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective blocker, and using it before alpha-blockade still risks unopposed alpha stimulation and loss of compensatory heart rate and contractility. It is not the first drug in this setting.

D.reason: Hydrochlorothiazide is used for primary hypertension and has no role in controlling catecholamine-driven crises. It also does not block the receptors responsible for his symptoms.

E.reason: ACE inhibitors are used for primary hypertension, heart failure, and diabetes, but they do not block catecholamine receptors. They would not safely control this patient's perioperative blood pressure.

high_yield_pearl: Pheochromocytoma: alpha-blocker first, then beta-blocker.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Catecholamine-secreting tumor; unopposed alpha stimulation is dangerous if beta-blockers are given first.
-  Clinical Findings: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, severe hypertension.
-  Diagnostics: Plasma or urine metanephrines; adrenal imaging.
-  Management: Phentolamine or phenoxybenzamine (alpha-blockade first) prior to resection, then beta-blockade.

stem: A 58-year-old man with stable angina and erectile dysfunction takes sildenafil 2 hours before sexual activity. During intercourse he develops substernal chest pressure and takes a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet. Ten minutes later he becomes lightheaded and diaphoretic, with a blood pressure of 62/38 mm Hg and heart rate of 118/min. His ECG shows no ST elevation, and troponin is normal. Which of the following best explains his hypotension?
option_A: Additive increase in cGMP causing profound vasodilation
option_C: Release of cyanide from the nitrate
option_E: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle
correct_explanation: Nitrates release nitric oxide in vascular smooth muscle, which increases cGMP and causes smooth muscle relaxation, dilating veins more than arteries and decreasing preload. Sildenafil inhibits PDE-5, the enzyme that degrades cGMP. When the two are combined, cGMP rises markedly, causing profound vasodilation and severe hypotension. This is why nitrates are contraindicated with concurrent PDE-5 inhibitor use, along with right ventricular infarction and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The reflex tachycardia reflects the compensatory sympathetic response.

B.reason: Methemoglobinemia is a recognized adverse effect of nitrates, but it presents with cyanosis and a low oxygen saturation despite normal PaO2, not isolated profound hypotension. The timing after sildenafil points to a cGMP interaction.

C.reason: Cyanide release is a toxicity of sodium nitroprusside, not of nitroglycerin. It would present with lactic acidosis and altered mental status.

D.reason: Nitrate tolerance reduces the effect of the drug with continuous exposure and does not cause hypotension. Monday disease refers to loss of tolerance over a weekend with headache and tachycardia upon re-exposure, not a drug interaction.

E.reason: Blockade of L-type calcium channels is the mechanism of calcium channel blockers, not nitrates or sildenafil. The interaction here involves the NO-cGMP pathway.

high_yield_pearl: Nitrates plus PDE-5 inhibitors cause life-threatening hypotension through additive cGMP.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate) vasodilate by releasing NO in vascular smooth muscle, increasing cGMP and causing smooth muscle relaxation; veins dilate more than arteries, decreasing preload.
-  Clinical Findings: Used for angina, ACS, pulmonary edema. Adverse effects: reflex tachycardia, methemoglobinemia, hypotension, flushing, headache, Monday disease.
-  Diagnostics: N/A.
-  Management: Contraindicated in right ventricular infarction, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and with PDE-5 inhibitors.

stem: A 52-year-old man with hypertensive emergency presents with severe headache and confusion. Blood pressure is 232/142 mm Hg, funduscopy shows papilledema with flame hemorrhages, and creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL. He is started on a sodium nitroprusside infusion with good blood pressure control. After 48 hours of continuous infusion, he becomes progressively more confused and tachypneic, with a serum bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L and an elevated lactate. His blood pressure is now 134/84 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
option_A: Cyanide toxicity
correct_explanation: Severe hypertension with encephalopathy, papilledema, and rising creatinine is a hypertensive emergency, and nitroprusside is a short-acting vasodilator of arteries and veins. It acts through direct release of nitric oxide, which raises cGMP. Nitroprusside also releases cyanide, and prolonged infusion, especially with renal impairment, can cause cyanide toxicity. Cyanide inhibits cellular respiration, causing lactic acidosis, tachypnea, and altered mental status as seen in this patient. Alternative agents for hypertensive emergency include labetalol, clevidipine, fenoldopam, and nicardipine.

B.reason: Drug-induced lupus is an adverse effect of hydralazine and presents with arthralgias, rash, and antihistone antibodies over weeks. It does not cause acute lactic acidosis.

C.reason: Reflex tachycardia with angina is an adverse effect of hydralazine, which is contraindicated in angina or CAD. It does not cause metabolic acidosis and confusion.

D.reason: Hyperprolactinemia is an adverse effect of verapamil, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. It is not associated with nitroprusside.

E.reason: Gingival hyperplasia is a calcium channel blocker adverse effect that develops over months. It would not cause acute confusion and lactic acidosis.

high_yield_pearl: Prolonged nitroprusside infusion can release cyanide and cause lactic acidosis.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Nitroprusside is a short-acting vasodilator of arteries and veins via direct NO release, increasing cGMP; it releases cyanide.
-  Clinical Findings: Cyanide toxicity: confusion, metabolic acidosis. Hypertensive emergency: severe hypertension with acute end-organ damage.
-  Diagnostics: Lactate, bicarbonate; blood pressure monitoring.
-  Management: Hypertensive emergency: labetalol, clevidipine, fenoldopam, nicardipine, nitroprusside; limit nitroprusside duration.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with chronic stable angina continues to have exertional chest pain despite maximally tolerated metoprolol, amlodipine, and long-acting isosorbide mononitrate. Heart rate is 58/min and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg, which limits further titration of her current drugs. Her physician adds a drug that relieves angina without changing heart rate or blood pressure. ECG shows a QTc of 462 msec. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of this drug?
option_A: Inhibition of the late phase of the inward sodium current
option_B: Inhibition of the funny sodium current (If) in the sinoatrial node
option_C: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle
option_D: Release of nitric oxide with increased smooth muscle cGMP
correct_explanation: Refractory angina despite maximal beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker, and nitrate therapy, with blood pressure and heart rate limiting further titration, calls for an agent that does not affect hemodynamics. Ranolazine inhibits the late phase of the inward sodium current, which reduces diastolic wall tension and myocardial oxygen consumption. It does not affect heart rate or blood pressure, so it can be added without worsening bradycardia or hypotension. It is indicated for refractory angina, and its adverse effects include constipation, dizziness, headache, nausea, and QT prolongation. The baseline QTc of 462 msec warrants monitoring.

B.reason: Inhibition of If in the sinoatrial node is the mechanism of ivabradine, which lowers heart rate and is used in chronic HFrEF. This patient already has a heart rate of 58/min, and the described drug leaves rate unchanged.

C.reason: L-type calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine reduce vascular tone and contractility. She is already taking amlodipine and the added drug acts differently.

D.reason: Release of nitric oxide with increased cGMP is the mechanism of nitrates, which she takes as isosorbide mononitrate. They lower preload and blood pressure, unlike the added agent.

E.reason: Beta-1 blockade is the mechanism of metoprolol, which she takes and which lowers heart rate and blood pressure. The added drug does not change these parameters.

high_yield_pearl: Ranolazine blocks the late Na+ current and treats refractory angina without changing HR or BP.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Inhibits the late phase of the inward sodium current, reducing diastolic wall tension and oxygen consumption; no effect on HR or BP.
-  Clinical Findings: Used for refractory angina.
-  Diagnostics: Monitor ECG for QT prolongation.
-  Management: Adverse effects: constipation, dizziness, headache, nausea, QT prolongation.

stem: A 66-year-old man with HFrEF and an ejection fraction of 25% has been taking lisinopril for 2 years. His cardiologist switches him to sacubitril-valsartan, and he takes the first dose the same evening as his last lisinopril dose. Two hours later he develops swelling of his lips and tongue with a muffled voice. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, and there is no urticaria or wheezing. Which of the following best explains this reaction?
option_A: Accumulation of bradykinin from combined ACE and neprilysin inhibition
option_C: Hyperkalemia from the angiotensin receptor blocker component
correct_explanation: Swelling of the lips and tongue without urticaria or bronchospasm shortly after starting a neprilysin inhibitor on top of an ACE inhibitor is angioedema. Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, which prevents degradation of bradykinin, natriuretic peptides, angiotensin II, and substance P, producing vasodilation and decreased ECF volume. ACE inhibitors also raise bradykinin by blocking its breakdown. When both are present, bradykinin accumulates and causes angioedema, so sacubitril-valsartan is contraindicated with ACE inhibitors. It is used in combination with the ARB valsartan to treat HFrEF.

B.reason: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causes urticaria, wheezing, and anaphylactic features. This patient has isolated angioedema without urticaria, which fits bradykinin-mediated swelling.

C.reason: Hyperkalemia is an adverse effect of the ARB component but presents with ECG changes and weakness, not tongue and lip swelling. It does not explain this reaction.

D.reason: Hypotension is a known adverse effect of sacubitril-valsartan, but this patient's blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Hypotension does not cause lip and tongue swelling.

E.reason: Bradykinin levels rise, not fall, with both neprilysin and ACE inhibition. A depletion mechanism would not produce angioedema.

high_yield_pearl: Never combine sacubitril with an ACE inhibitor: bradykinin buildup causes angioedema.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Neprilysin inhibitor prevents degradation of bradykinin, natriuretic peptides, angiotensin II, and substance P, causing vasodilation and decreased ECF volume.
-  Clinical Findings: Adverse effects: hypotension, hyperkalemia (from ARB), cough, dizziness; angioedema with ACE inhibitors.
-  Diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis.
-  Management: Used with valsartan in HFrEF; contraindicated with ACE inhibitors.

stem: A 58-year-old man is started on atorvastatin after an anterior MI, and his LDL cholesterol falls from 168 to 74 mg/dL over 8 weeks. He has no muscle symptoms, and his liver enzymes remain normal. His physician explains that the drug reduces LDL by changing hepatocyte cholesterol handling. Which of the following hepatic changes is primarily responsible for the fall in LDL?
option_A: Increased LDL receptor recycling in response to decreased intrahepatic cholesterol
option_C: Blocked cholesterol absorption at the brush border
option_E: Decreased hormone-sensitive lipase activity in adipose tissue
correct_explanation: Statins such as atorvastatin inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, and decrease intrahepatic cholesterol. The hepatocyte compensates by increasing LDL receptor recycling, which increases LDL catabolism and lowers serum LDL. This effect reduces plaque progression and the risk of plaque rupture, and statins decrease mortality in patients with CAD. Adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, so LFTs are monitored, and myopathy, particularly when combined with fibrates or niacin. This patient has had no muscle symptoms.

B.reason: Disrupting enterohepatic bile acid circulation is the mechanism of bile acid resins such as cholestyramine, which cause compensatory conversion of cholesterol to bile. Atorvastatin acts on synthesis.

C.reason: Blocking cholesterol absorption at the small intestine brush border is the mechanism of ezetimibe. Atorvastatin inhibits hepatic synthesis.

D.reason: Upregulation of lipoprotein lipase is the action of fibrates, which activate PPAR-alpha and mainly lower triglycerides. It is not the primary mechanism for lowering LDL with a statin.

E.reason: Inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue is the mechanism of niacin, which reduces hepatic VLDL synthesis. It is not how statins lower LDL.

high_yield_pearl: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, raising LDL receptor recycling and lowering LDL.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Statins (atorvastatin, lovastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin) inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, decreasing intrahepatic cholesterol and increasing LDL receptor recycling and LDL catabolism.
-  Clinical Findings: Decrease LDL, plaque progression, and mortality in CAD.
-  Diagnostics: Monitor LFTs.
-  Management: Adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, myopathy (especially with fibrates or niacin).

stem: A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is hospitalized with acute pancreatitis. His fasting triglyceride level is 1,240 mg/dL, and lipemic serum is noted. After recovery, he is started on gemfibrozil for long-term triglyceride lowering. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of this drug?
option_A: Activation of PPAR-alpha with upregulation of lipoprotein lipase
option_C: Inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue
option_E: Disruption of enterohepatic bile acid circulation
correct_explanation: A triglyceride level above 1,000 mg/dL causing pancreatitis requires a drug that lowers triglycerides effectively. Fibrates such as gemfibrozil and fenofibrate activate PPAR-alpha, which upregulates lipoprotein lipase and increases triglyceride clearance. PPAR-alpha activation also induces HDL synthesis. Fibrates carry a risk of myopathy, especially when combined with statins, and can cause cholesterol gallstones through inhibition of cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase. They lower triglycerides much more than LDL.

B.reason: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is the mechanism of statins, which mostly lower LDL. Statins have a smaller effect on severe hypertriglyceridemia.

C.reason: Inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue is the mechanism of niacin, which reduces hepatic VLDL synthesis. It is not the mechanism of gemfibrozil.

D.reason: Preventing LDL receptor degradation is the mechanism of PCSK9 inhibitors such as alirocumab and evolocumab, which lower LDL. It does not address chylomicron and VLDL triglyceride clearance.

E.reason: Disrupting enterohepatic bile acid circulation is the mechanism of bile acid resins, which lower LDL and can modestly raise triglycerides. They are inappropriate for severe hypertriglyceridemia.

high_yield_pearl: Fibrates activate PPAR-alpha, raise LPL, and clear triglycerides; watch for myopathy with statins and gallstones.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Fenofibrate, gemfibrozil activate PPAR-alpha, upregulating LPL and increasing TG clearance; also induce HDL synthesis.
-  Clinical Findings: Main effect is lowering triglycerides.
-  Diagnostics: Lipid panel.
-  Management: Adverse effects: myopathy risk with statins, cholesterol gallstones via inhibition of cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase.

stem: A 41-year-old man with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has tendinous xanthomas on his Achilles tendons and a prior MI at age 38. Despite maximally tolerated rosuvastatin and ezetimibe, his LDL cholesterol remains 142 mg/dL. His physician adds a subcutaneous injectable monoclonal antibody, and 12 weeks later the LDL falls to 62 mg/dL. Which of the following is the mechanism by which this drug lowers LDL?
option_A: Prevention of LDL receptor degradation, increasing LDL receptor recycling and hepatic LDL uptake
option_B: Inhibition of cholesterol absorption at the small intestine brush border
option_C: Activation of PPAR-alpha and upregulation of lipoprotein lipase
option_D: Inhibition of lipolysis in adipose tissue
option_E: Binding of bile acids in the intestinal lumen
correct_explanation: A young patient with tendinous xanthomas, premature MI, and persistent LDL elevation on statin and ezetimibe has familial hypercholesterolemia requiring additional therapy. PCSK9 inhibitors such as alirocumab and evolocumab are monoclonal antibodies that bind PCSK9, which normally promotes LDL receptor degradation. Blocking PCSK9 prevents LDL receptor degradation, increases LDL receptor recycling, and increases hepatic LDL uptake, which lowers serum LDL and reduces atherosclerosis. These agents are not metabolized by CYP enzymes and have minimal drug interactions. Their adverse effects are limited.

B.reason: Preventing cholesterol absorption at the brush border is the mechanism of ezetimibe, which this patient already takes. The added injectable acts through a different pathway.

C.reason: PPAR-alpha activation with LPL upregulation is the mechanism of fibrates, which primarily lower triglycerides. They do not substantially lower LDL.

D.reason: Inhibition of lipolysis through hormone-sensitive lipase is the mechanism of niacin, which lowers VLDL synthesis. It is an oral drug, not a monoclonal antibody.

E.reason: Binding of bile acids is the mechanism of resins such as cholestyramine, which are oral and not antibodies. They would not be injected subcutaneously.

high_yield_pearl: PCSK9 inhibitors block LDL receptor degradation to lower LDL, with minimal drug interactions.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Alirocumab, evolocumab inhibit PCSK9, preventing LDL receptor degradation and increasing LDL receptor recycling and hepatic LDL uptake, lowering serum LDL.
-  Clinical Findings: Tendinous xanthomas are associated with familial hypercholesterolemia.
-  Diagnostics: Lipid panel.
-  Management: No CYP metabolism and minimal drug interactions; add-on for refractory LDL elevation.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with HFrEF, atrial fibrillation, and chronic kidney disease takes digoxin, furosemide, and, since last week, verapamil for rate control. She presents with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and blurry, yellow-tinted vision. Heart rate is 118/min, and ECG shows atrial tachycardia with AV block. Serum potassium is 6.2 mEq/L and creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
option_A: Anti-digoxin Fab fragments
correct_explanation: Gastrointestinal symptoms, yellow-tinted vision, atrial tachycardia with AV block, and hyperkalemia in a patient on digoxin are signs of digoxin toxicity. Digoxin directly inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase, which raises extracellular potassium, and hyperkalemia indicates a poor prognosis. Toxicity is favored by renal failure, which reduces excretion, hypokalemia, and drugs that displace digoxin or decrease its clearance, such as verapamil, amiodarone, and quinidine. The antidote is anti-digoxin Fab fragments, with slow normalization of K+, a cardiac pacer if needed, and Mg2+. Hyperkalemia here is a marker of severe toxicity.

B.reason: Potassium repletion is appropriate for hypokalemia, which predisposes to toxicity, but this patient is already hyperkalemic at 6.2 mEq/L. Giving potassium would worsen the hyperkalemia.

C.reason: Verapamil decreases digoxin clearance and displaces it from tissue-binding sites, so it likely precipitated this toxicity. More verapamil would worsen both toxicity and AV block.

D.reason: Quinidine decreases digoxin clearance and raises levels, and it is a class IA drug that can itself cause arrhythmias. It would worsen toxicity.

E.reason: Amiodarone also raises digoxin levels by decreasing clearance and causes bradycardia and heart block. It would worsen this patient's AV block.

high_yield_pearl: Digoxin toxicity with hyperkalemia: give anti-digoxin Fab and avoid verapamil, amiodarone, and quinidine.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Direct inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase leads to indirect inhibition of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, increased intracellular Ca2+, positive inotropy; stimulates the vagus nerve, decreasing HR.
-  Clinical Findings: Cholinergic effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), blurry yellow vision, arrhythmias, atrial tachycardia with AV block; hyperkalemia indicates poor prognosis. Predisposing: renal failure, hypokalemia, displacing drugs (verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine).
-  Diagnostics: Digoxin level, K+, ECG.
-  Management: Slowly normalize K+, cardiac pacer, anti-digoxin Fab fragments, Mg2+.

concept_name: Antiarrhythmics: class IA sodium channel blockers
stem: A 62-year-old man has been taking procainamide for 8 months for recurrent ventricular arrhythmias. He now has joint pain in his hands and knees, pleuritic chest pain, and a low-grade fever. Examination shows a pleural friction rub and symmetric wrist swelling. Serum antihistone antibodies are positive, and his anti-dsDNA is negative. Which of the following adverse effects explains his presentation?
option_A: Reversible SLE-like syndrome
correct_explanation: Arthralgias, pleuritis, and fever with antihistone antibodies months after starting procainamide indicate drug-induced lupus. Procainamide is a class IA sodium channel blocker that causes moderate Na+ channel blockade, increases action potential duration, effective refractory period, and QT interval, and has some K+ channel-blocking effects. Its adverse effects include a reversible SLE-like syndrome, whereas quinidine causes cinchonism (headache, tinnitus) and disopyramide causes heart failure. The syndrome resolves after the drug is stopped.

B.reason: Cinchonism, with headache and tinnitus, is an adverse effect of quinidine, another class IA drug. It does not cause arthritis, pleuritis, or antihistone antibodies.

C.reason: Heart failure exacerbation is an adverse effect of disopyramide because of its negative inotropy. This patient has systemic inflammatory features, not worsening cardiac function.

D.reason: Gingival hyperplasia is an adverse effect of calcium channel blockers. It does not cause serologic autoimmunity.

E.reason: Pulmonary fibrosis is an adverse effect of amiodarone and presents with progressive dyspnea and dry cough. This patient's pleuritic pain with arthritis and antihistone antibodies fits lupus.

high_yield_pearl: Procainamide causes drug-induced lupus with antihistone antibodies.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Class IA (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) causes moderate Na+ channel blockade, increasing AP duration, ERP, and QT interval; some K+ channel blocking effects.
-  Clinical Findings: Used for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, especially reentrant and ectopic SVT and VT. Adverse effects: cinchonism (quinidine), reversible SLE-like syndrome (procainamide), HF (disopyramide).
-  Diagnostics: Antihistone antibodies in drug-induced lupus.
-  Management: Stop the drug.

concept_name: Antiarrhythmics: class IC sodium channel blockers
stem: A 63-year-old man with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and a prior inferior MI 2 years ago presents with palpitations. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg and heart rate is 118/min and irregularly irregular. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 52% with an old inferior scar. His physician is choosing a rhythm or rate control agent. Which of the following drugs should be avoided in this patient?
option_A: Flecainide
correct_explanation: This patient has atrial fibrillation with structural, ischemic heart disease from a prior MI. Class IC drugs, flecainide and propafenone, strongly block Na+ channels and significantly prolong the ERP in the AV node and accessory bypass tracts, with minimal effect on action potential duration. They are used for SVTs, including atrial fibrillation. They are proarrhythmic, especially post-MI, and are contraindicated in structural and ischemic heart disease. Beta-blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and digoxin are acceptable for rate control, so flecainide is the drug to avoid.

B.reason: Beta-blockers such as metoprolol provide ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation and help prevent ventricular arrhythmias post-MI. They are appropriate and beneficial for this patient.

C.reason: Diltiazem, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, provides rate control in atrial fibrillation. With a preserved ejection fraction it is acceptable, though it should be used cautiously in heart failure.

D.reason: Digoxin decreases conduction at the AV node and is part of the rate-control regimen for atrial fibrillation. It is not contraindicated by his ischemic scar.

E.reason: Sotalol is a class III potassium channel blocker used for atrial fibrillation. It requires monitoring for torsades de pointes, but it is not contraindicated by structural heart disease in the way class IC drugs are.

high_yield_pearl: Class IC drugs are contraindicated in structural or ischemic heart disease, especially post-MI.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Class IC (flecainide, propafenone): strong Na+ channel blockade; significantly prolongs ERP in AV node and accessory bypass tracts; no effect on ERP in Purkinje and ventricular tissue; minimal effect on AP duration.
-  Clinical Findings: Used for SVTs including atrial fibrillation; last resort in refractory VT.
-  Diagnostics: ECG; echocardiography for structural disease.
-  Management: Proarrhythmic, especially post-MI; contraindicated in structural and ischemic heart disease.

concept_name: Antiarrhythmics: class II beta-blockers and overdose
stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after ingesting an unknown quantity of her father's metoprolol tablets 3 hours ago. She is drowsy, with a heart rate of 36/min and blood pressure of 68/40 mm Hg. Her extremities are cool, lung fields are clear, and fingerstick glucose is 52 mg/dL. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with first-degree AV block. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic treatment?
option_A: Glucagon
correct_explanation: Bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, and hypoglycemia after ingestion of a beta-blocker indicate beta-blocker overdose. Beta-blockers decrease SA and AV nodal activity by decreasing cAMP and Ca2+ currents, slow the slope of phase 4, and prolong the PR interval. Toxicity produces bradycardia, AV block, heart failure, and CNS depression, and beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia signs. Treatment of beta-blocker overdose is Glucagon, Atropine, and Saline (GAS). Glucagon bypasses the blocked beta receptor by raising cAMP through its own receptor, restoring inotropy and chronotropy.

B.reason: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity, which causes miosis and respiratory depression. This patient's bradycardia, hypotension, and AV block follow a beta-blocker ingestion.

C.reason: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine toxicity and is not appropriate for a beta-blocker overdose. It also carries a seizure risk.

D.reason: Phenylephrine is an alpha-agonist that raises blood pressure by vasoconstriction but does not reverse bradycardia or the depressed contractility from beta-blockade. It could further increase afterload on a failing heart.

E.reason: Digoxin slows AV node conduction and would worsen bradycardia and AV block. It is not an antidote for beta-blocker overdose.

high_yield_pearl: Beta-blocker overdose: GAS (Glucagon, Atropine, Saline).
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Class II beta-blockers (metoprolol, propranolol, esmolol, atenolol, timolol, carvedilol) decrease SA and AV nodal activity by decreasing cAMP and Ca2+ currents; suppress abnormal pacemakers by decreasing the slope of phase 4; prolong the PR interval.
-  Clinical Findings: Adverse effects: impotence, bronchospasm in COPD and asthma, bradycardia, AV block, HF, sedation; may mask hypoglycemia.
-  Diagnostics: ECG, glucose.
-  Management: Overdose treated with glucagon, atropine, saline.

concept_name: Antiarrhythmics: class IB sodium channel blockers
stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted 6 hours after the onset of chest pain, and ECG shows anterior ST elevation. During transfer to the catheterization laboratory he develops sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 168/min. He is conscious and blood pressure is 106/64 mm Hg. His physician selects a sodium channel blocker that preferentially affects ischemic or depolarized myocardium. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate?
option_A: Lidocaine
correct_explanation: Sustained ventricular tachycardia in the setting of acute MI requires an antiarrhythmic that suppresses ventricular ectopy in ischemic myocardium. Class IB drugs, lidocaine and mexiletine, cause weak Na+ channel blockade and decrease the action potential duration. They preferentially affect ischemic or depolarized Purkinje and ventricular tissue, where Na+ channels are more often in the depolarized state. They are used for acute ventricular arrhythmias, especially post-MI, and for digitalis-induced arrhythmias, and IB is best post-MI. Adverse effects include CNS stimulation or depression and cardiovascular depression.

B.reason: Flecainide is a class IC drug that is proarrhythmic post-MI and is contraindicated in ischemic heart disease. It would be dangerous in this patient.

C.reason: Quinidine is a class IA drug that prolongs the QT interval and can provoke torsades de pointes. It is not preferred for ischemic ventricular tachycardia.

D.reason: Sotalol is a class III potassium channel blocker that prolongs repolarization and can cause torsades de pointes, and its beta-blocking effect could worsen acute hemodynamics. It does not preferentially act on ischemic tissue.

E.reason: Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for rate control and nodal arrhythmias. It is not used for ventricular tachycardia in acute MI and can cause hypotension and cardiac depression.

high_yield_pearl: Class IB (lidocaine) is best post-MI and for digitalis-induced arrhythmias.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Class IB (lidocaine, mexiletine): weak Na+ channel blockade; decreases AP duration; preferentially affects ischemic or depolarized Purkinje and ventricular tissue.
-  Clinical Findings: Used for acute ventricular arrhythmias, especially post-MI, and digitalis-induced arrhythmias.
-  Diagnostics: ECG.
-  Management: Adverse effects: CNS stimulation or depression, cardiovascular depression.

concept_name: Antiarrhythmics: class III potassium channel blockers (amiodarone)
stem: A 61-year-old man with recurrent ventricular tachycardia has taken amiodarone for 2 years. He reports fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and a new dry cough. Examination shows blue-gray discoloration of sun-exposed skin and corneal deposits on slit-lamp examination. TSH is 14 mIU/L with a low free T4, and chest radiograph shows interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following properties best explains his thyroid abnormality?
option_A: High iodine content of the drug
option_C: Class IV calcium channel blocking effect
correct_explanation: Amiodarone is a class III potassium channel blocker that increases action potential duration, ERP, and QT interval and is used in atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, and ventricular tachycardia. It is about 40% iodine by weight, and the iodine load can cause either hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, as seen here with an elevated TSH and low free T4. Other adverse effects include pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, corneal deposits, blue-gray skin deposits with photodermatitis, neurologic effects, constipation, bradycardia, heart block, and heart failure. Because of this toxicity, PFTs, LFTs, and TFTs should be checked when using amiodarone. The drug is lipophilic and has class I, II, III, and IV effects.

B.reason: The class II beta-blocking effect of amiodarone contributes to bradycardia and AV block but does not alter thyroid hormone synthesis. It does not explain the elevated TSH.

C.reason: The class IV calcium channel-blocking effect contributes to bradycardia, heart block, and constipation. It is not responsible for hypothyroidism.

D.reason: Acting as a hapten is a proposed contributor to amiodarone's pulmonary and other tissue toxicity, which could explain the interstitial infiltrates. It does not explain the thyroid abnormality.

E.reason: QT prolongation predisposes to torsades de pointes and has nothing to do with thyroid function. This patient has no ventricular arrhythmia described and the question concerns his endocrine finding.

high_yield_pearl: Amiodarone is 40% iodine: check PFTs, LFTs, and TFTs.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Class III (amiodarone, ibutilide, dofetilide, sotalol) block K+ channels, increasing AP duration, ERP, and QT interval. Amiodarone is lipophilic, 40% iodine by weight, with class I, II, III, and IV effects.
-  Clinical Findings: Amiodarone: pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, corneal deposits, blue-gray skin, neurologic effects, constipation, bradycardia, heart block, HF. Sotalol and ibutilide: torsades de pointes.
-  Diagnostics: Check PFTs, LFTs, TFTs.
-  Management: Used for atrial fibrillation, flutter, and ventricular tachycardia.

stem: A 59-year-old man with HFrEF (ejection fraction 30%) in normal sinus rhythm remains symptomatic with a resting heart rate of 84/min despite maximally tolerated metoprolol succinate, an ACE inhibitor, and spironolactone. His blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. His physician adds ivabradine, and at his 2-week visit he reports that he sees transient bright flashes of light, especially when moving from dark to light environments. Which of the following best describes the mechanism and this adverse effect of the drug?
option_A: Inhibition of the funny sodium current in the SA node; luminous phenomena
option_B: Inhibition of L-type calcium channels; gingival hyperplasia
option_C: Inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase; yellow-tinted vision
option_E: Inhibition of the late sodium current; QT prolongation
correct_explanation: A patient with chronic HFrEF in sinus rhythm with a persistently elevated heart rate despite beta-blocker therapy is a candidate for ivabradine. Ivabradine prolongs the slow depolarization of phase 4 by selectively inhibiting the funny sodium channels (If) in the SA node, thereby lowering heart rate without affecting contractility. Its adverse effects include luminous phenomena (visual brightness), hypertension, bradycardia, and torsades de pointes due to QT prolongation. The patient's transient bright flashes with changes in lighting are characteristic of luminous phenomena. Yellow-tinted vision belongs to digoxin toxicity.

B.reason: Inhibition of L-type calcium channels with gingival hyperplasia describes calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem. Ivabradine does not act on calcium channels.

C.reason: Inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase with yellow-tinted vision describes digoxin toxicity. Ivabradine acts on the funny current, and the visual symptom described is brightness, not yellow tint.

D.reason: Inhibition of neprilysin with angioedema describes sacubitril. It is combined with valsartan in HFrEF but is not related to the visual symptoms here.

E.reason: Inhibition of the late sodium current with QT prolongation describes ranolazine, used in refractory angina. It does not lower heart rate or cause luminous phenomena.

high_yield_pearl: Ivabradine blocks If in the SA node and causes luminous visual phenomena.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Ivabradine prolongs slow depolarization phase 4 by selectively inhibiting funny sodium channels (If).
-  Clinical Findings: Used for chronic HFrEF; adverse effects: luminous phenomena (visual brightness), hypertension, bradycardia, torsades de pointes due to QT prolongation.
-  Diagnostics: Heart rate and ECG monitoring.
-  Management: Added to guideline therapy when the heart rate remains elevated in sinus rhythm.

concept_name: Heart anatomy: right ventricle and left atrium
stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after a stab wound to the left parasternal chest at the fourth intercostal space. Blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg and heart rate is 128/min, with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. A bedside ultrasound shows a pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of one chamber. At emergency thoracotomy, the surgeon finds the laceration in the cardiac chamber that lies most anteriorly in the chest. Which chamber was most likely injured?
option_A: Right ventricle
correct_explanation: A parasternal stab wound with hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, and an effusion with chamber collapse indicates cardiac tamponade from penetrating trauma. The chamber that lies most anteriorly in the thorax is the right ventricle, which is therefore the chamber most commonly injured in trauma. The left atrium, in contrast, is the most posterior part of the heart, which is why its enlargement can compress the esophagus and left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The left ventricle forms about two thirds and the right ventricle about one third of the inferior (diaphragmatic) cardiac surface. Blood leaking from the right ventricle fills the pericardial sac and produces the Beck triad.

B.reason: The left ventricle lies more posteriorly and to the left, so a left parasternal wound is less likely to reach it first. It is also protected by a thicker wall that is more likely to seal small injuries.

C.reason: The right atrium forms the right heart border and lies to the right of the sternum. A left parasternal wound is unlikely to reach it before traversing the right ventricle.

D.reason: The left atrium is the most posterior chamber, lying against the esophagus. It would be injured only by a deep posterior wound or one through the left ventricle.

E.reason: The ascending aorta is a great vessel, not a cardiac chamber, and an injury would cause rapid exsanguination rather than a contained tamponade. The question asks for the chamber that is most anterior.

high_yield_pearl: The RV is the most anterior chamber and most often injured; the LA is the most posterior.
topic_overview:
- Etiology/Pathophysiology: LA is the most posterior part of the heart; RV is the most anterior and most commonly injured in trauma. LV forms about 2/3 and RV about 1/3 of the inferior surface.
- Clinical Findings: LA enlargement can cause dysphagia and hoarseness (Ortner syndrome); RV injury can cause tamponade.
- Diagnostics: Chest radiograph, echocardiography.
- Management: Emergency drainage or repair for traumatic tamponade.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents with 50 minutes of crushing chest pain and diaphoresis. Heart rate is 40/min and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with complete AV block. Angiography shows a left-dominant coronary circulation, and the posterior descending artery arises from the left circumflex artery. Which of the following vessels is most likely occluded?
option_A: Left circumflex artery
correct_explanation: ST elevation in II, III, and aVF indicates an inferior infarct, and complete AV block indicates involvement of the artery that supplies the AV node. The posterior descending artery supplies the posterior one third of the interventricular septum, the posterior two thirds of the ventricular walls, the posteromedial papillary muscle, and the SA and AV nodes, depending on dominance. In left-dominant circulation (about 5–10% of patients), the PDA arises from the left circumflex artery rather than the RCA. Occlusion of the LCX in this patient therefore causes inferior infarction with nodal dysfunction. In the more common right-dominant pattern the RCA would be the culprit.

B.reason: The RCA gives rise to the PDA only in right-dominant circulation, which is the most common pattern. In this patient angiography shows left dominance, so the RCA does not supply the inferior wall and AV node.

C.reason: LAD occlusion causes anterior and septal infarction with ST elevation in the precordial leads. It would not produce inferior ST elevation with AV block in a left-dominant system.

D.reason: Left main occlusion causes extensive anterolateral ischemia, commonly with cardiogenic shock and widespread ST changes. The pattern here is limited to the inferior leads.

E.reason: The acute marginal artery supplies the right ventricle and arises from the RCA. Its occlusion would not cause AV block from loss of PDA supply.

high_yield_pearl: The PDA supplies the AV node: it comes from the RCA in right dominance and the LCX in left dominance.
topic_overview:
- Etiology/Pathophysiology: LAD supplies the anterior 2/3 of the septum, anterolateral papillary muscle, and anterior LV; PDA supplies the posterior 1/3 of the septum, posterior 2/3 of the ventricular walls, posteromedial papillary muscle, and SA and AV nodes. Dominance: right (most common, PDA from RCA), left (PDA from LCX, 5–10%), codominant (10–20%).
- Clinical Findings: PDA infarction can cause bradycardia or heart block.
- Diagnostics: ECG localization; coronary angiography.
- Management: Reperfusion.

concept_name: Cardiac output variables: preload and afterload
stem: A 57-year-old man with HFrEF (ejection fraction 30%) has exertional dyspnea and peripheral edema. Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg, heart rate is 84/min, and jugular venous pressure is elevated. His physician starts a drug that lowers both ventricular filling pressure and systemic arterial resistance. Which of the following drug classes has this combined effect?
option_A: ACE inhibitors
correct_explanation: This patient has systolic heart failure with congestion and elevated blood pressure, so reducing both preload and afterload is desirable. Preload is approximated by end-diastolic volume and depends on venous tone and circulating blood volume. Afterload is approximated by mean arterial pressure. ACE inhibitors and ARBs decrease both preload and afterload, in addition to their neurohormonal and mortality benefits in HFrEF. Venous vasodilators such as nitroglycerin lower preload only, whereas arterial vasodilators such as hydralazine lower afterload only.

B.reason: Nitroglycerin is a venous vasodilator and lowers preload predominantly. It has little direct effect on afterload at usual doses.

C.reason: Hydralazine is an arterial vasodilator that lowers afterload but does not reduce preload. It also causes reflex tachycardia, which would be undesirable in this patient.

D.reason: Dobutamine increases contractility through beta-1 stimulation and is used in cardiogenic shock. It does not lower preload and afterload in this manner and can increase myocardial oxygen demand.

E.reason: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist that increases afterload by vasoconstriction. This would worsen his heart failure.

high_yield_pearl: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower both preload and afterload; nitrates lower preload; hydralazine lowers afterload.
topic_overview:
- Etiology/Pathophysiology: SV is affected by contractility, afterload, and preload (SV CAP). Preload approximated by EDV; venous vasodilators (nitroglycerin) decrease preload. Afterload approximated by MAP; arterial vasodilators (hydralazine) decrease afterload; ACEi and ARBs decrease both.
- Clinical Findings: Chronic hypertension leads to LV hypertrophy.
- Diagnostics: Echocardiography, hemodynamics.
- Management: Match the agent to the hemodynamic target.

stem: A 38-year-old man with severe chronic aortic regurgitation has progressive dyspnea and exertional chest pain despite normal coronary arteries on angiography. Echocardiography shows a markedly dilated left ventricle with an end-diastolic diameter of 7.4 cm and a normal wall thickness. His blood pressure is 156/48 mm Hg. According to the Laplace law, which of the following changes most directly increases his myocardial wall tension and oxygen demand?
option_A: Increased ventricular chamber radius
correct_explanation: Wall tension follows Laplace law: wall tension equals pressure multiplied by radius, and wall stress equals pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness. In chronic aortic regurgitation, volume overload dilates the left ventricle, so the chamber radius is markedly increased. A larger radius raises wall tension for any given pressure, and because the wall has not thickened in proportion, wall stress also rises. Myocardial oxygen demand is increased by contractility, afterload, heart rate, and ventricular diameter, which raises wall tension. This explains angina in a patient with normal coronary arteries.

B.reason: Increased wall thickness lowers wall stress, which is why the ventricle hypertrophies in response to high pressure. This patient has a normal wall thickness, so it is not the cause of his raised tension.

C.reason: Decreased pressure would reduce wall tension, since tension is proportional to pressure. His systolic pressure is elevated, not decreased.

D.reason: Decreased afterload reduces wall tension and oxygen demand. His afterload is increased with a blood pressure of 156/48 mm Hg.

E.reason: Increased contractility does raise oxygen demand but is not a variable in the Laplace equation. The question asks for the change that directly increases wall tension.

high_yield_pearl: Wall tension = pressure x radius, so a dilated ventricle has higher wall tension and oxygen demand.
topic_overview:
- Etiology/Pathophysiology: Wall tension = pressure x radius; wall stress = pressure x radius / (2 x wall thickness). Myocardial O2 demand is increased by contractility, afterload, heart rate, and ventricular diameter.
- Clinical Findings: Chronic pressure overload leads to concentric hypertrophy to decrease wall stress.
- Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
- Management: Reduce afterload and treat the underlying valve lesion.

concept_name: Cardiac output equations: stroke volume, ejection fraction, and cardiac output
stem: A 66-year-old woman with a prior anterior MI has exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. Her heart rate is 90/min and her blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular end-diastolic volume of 160 mL and an end-systolic volume of 100 mL. Her physician calculates her stroke volume, ejection fraction, and cardiac output. Which of the following sets of values is correct?
option_A: SV 60 mL; EF 38%; CO 5.4 L/min
correct_explanation: Stroke volume is end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume, so 160 minus 100 equals 60 mL. Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, 60/160, which is about 38% and well below the normal range of 50–70%. Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate, so 60 mL times 90 per minute equals 5,400 mL/min, or 5.4 L/min. The reduced EF after anterior MI indicates systolic heart failure with reduced contractility.

B.reason: An EF of 63% is the end-systolic volume subtracted from 1 using the wrong ratio (100/160 = 63%, which is ESV/EDV). The correct EF is SV/EDV, or 38%.

C.reason: A stroke volume of 100 mL is the end-systolic volume, mistakenly used as stroke volume. This inflates both the EF and the cardiac output.

D.reason: The SV and EF are correct, but a cardiac output of 14.4 L/min results from multiplying EDV (160 mL) by heart rate. Cardiac output depends on stroke volume.

E.reason: A stroke volume equal to the EDV would imply the ventricle ejects everything, giving an EF of 100%, which is physiologically impossible. This results from ignoring the end-systolic volume.

high_yield_pearl: SV = EDV - ESV; EF = SV/EDV; CO = SV x HR.
topic_overview:
- Etiology/Pathophysiology: SV = EDV - ESV; EF = SV/EDV (normal 50–70%); CO = SV x HR; Fick: CO = O2 consumption / (arterial O2 content - venous O2 content).
- Clinical Findings: EF is decreased in systolic HF and usually normal in diastolic HF.
- Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
- Management: Treat the underlying cause of systolic dysfunction.

concept_name: Pulse pressure: wide pulse pressure in high-output states
stem: A 26-year-old woman has 3 months of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, and a 6-kg weight loss. Blood pressure is 152/46 mm Hg and heart rate is 118/min, and her skin is warm and moist. Cardiac auscultation reveals no murmurs, and echocardiography shows normal valves with a hyperdynamic left ventricle. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. Which of the following best explains her wide pulse pressure?
option_A: Increased stroke volume
correct_explanation: Weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, tachycardia, and a suppressed TSH indicate hyperthyroidism, and the hyperdynamic ventricle with normal valves shows a high-output state. Pulse pressure is directly proportional to stroke volume and inversely proportional to arterial compliance. Thyroid hormone increases contractility and heart rate and lowers systemic vascular resistance, increasing stroke volume and systolic pressure while diastolic pressure falls. The pulse pressure of 106 mm Hg therefore reflects an increased stroke volume in a young patient with compliant arteries. Other causes of wide pulse pressure include aortic regurgitation, aortic stiffening in older adults, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia, and exercise.

B.reason: Decreased compliance from aortic stiffening explains isolated systolic hypertension in older adults. This is a young woman with a hyperdynamic circulation and no vascular disease.

C.reason: A decreased stroke volume narrows the pulse pressure, as in aortic stenosis, cardiac tamponade, cardiogenic shock, and advanced HF. Her ventricle is hyperdynamic.

D.reason: Increased arterial compliance would buffer the pressure change and narrow the pulse pressure. It is not the cause of her widened pressure.

E.reason: A decreased heart rate is not the mechanism, and her heart rate is high at 118/min. Pulse pressure is determined by stroke volume and compliance, not rate.

high_yield_pearl: High-output states (hyperthyroidism, anemia) widen pulse pressure by raising stroke volume.
topic_overview:
- Etiology/Pathophysiology: PP = SBP - DBP; directly proportional to SV, inversely proportional to arterial compliance. MAP = CO x TPR.
- Clinical Findings: Increased PP in aortic regurgitation, aortic stiffening, OSA, high-output states (anemia, hyperthyroidism), and exercise; decreased PP in aortic stenosis, cardiogenic shock, tamponade, advanced HF.
- Diagnostics: Blood pressure measurement; echocardiography.
- Management: Treat the underlying condition.

concept_name: Resistance, pressure, and flow: vessels in parallel
stem: A 61-year-old man on hemodialysis has had a left brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula for 5 years. He now has progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral edema. Blood pressure is 132/44 mm Hg and heart rate is 104/min, and a continuous thrill is palpable over the fistula. Echocardiography shows a dilated, hyperdynamic left ventricle with a cardiac output of 9.8 L/min. Which of the following best explains the physiologic effect of the fistula on his circulation?
option_A: Lower total resistance because the fistula adds a vascular bed in parallel
option_B: Higher total resistance because the fistula adds a resistor in series
option_C: Reduced venous return because of decreased capacitance
option_D: Increased blood viscosity from elevated hematocrit
correct_explanation: A dialysis patient with an arteriovenous fistula, a thrill, a hyperdynamic ventricle, and a cardiac output of 9.8 L/min has high-output heart failure. The fistula connects an artery directly to a vein and thus acts as a low-resistance pathway in parallel with the systemic capillary beds. For resistances in parallel, the reciprocal of total resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals, so total resistance falls below that of the lowest individual resistance. The lower SVR increases venous return and cardiac output, and the persistently high output eventually produces symptoms of congestion. First Aid lists arteriovenous shunting among the causes of high-output HF.

B.reason: Resistors in series add together and increase total resistance. The fistula is a parallel pathway, which has the opposite effect.

C.reason: Reduced venous capacitance would decrease venous return and cardiac output, whereas his cardiac output is elevated. The shunt increases venous return.

D.reason: Higher viscosity increases resistance, as in polycythemia, but dialysis patients are usually anemic, which lowers viscosity. The dominant effect here is the parallel shunt.

E.reason: Systemic vasoconstriction would increase SVR and decrease cardiac output. His low diastolic pressure and high output indicate vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.

high_yield_pearl: An AV shunt is a parallel resistance: it lowers SVR and can cause high-output heart failure.
topic_overview:
- Etiology/Pathophysiology: Resistance = driving pressure / flow = 8 x viscosity x length / (pi x r^4). Series: RT = R1 + R2 + R3. Parallel: 1/RT = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Arterioles account for most of TPR.
- Clinical Findings: High-output HF with decreased SVR: severe obesity, cirrhosis, anemia, hyperthyroidism, wet beriberi, Paget disease, AV shunting.
- Diagnostics: Echocardiography; hemodynamics.
- Management: Treat the underlying cause; reduce shunt flow if needed.

concept_name: Cardiac and vascular function curves: exercise
stem: A 28-year-old marathon runner undergoes cardiopulmonary exercise testing. At peak exertion, his cardiac output rises from 5.5 L/min to 28 L/min, and his mean arterial pressure rises modestly from 92 to 108 mm Hg. Calculated total peripheral resistance has fallen markedly. Which of the following combinations of changes best explains the increase in cardiac output at peak exercise?
option_A: Increased inotropy and decreased total peripheral resistance
option_B: Decreased inotropy and increased total peripheral resistance
option_C: Increased inotropy and increased total peripheral resistance
option_D: Decreased venous tone with decreased inotropy
correct_explanation: At peak exercise, cardiac output increases several-fold, with only a modest rise in blood pressure, implying a large fall in total peripheral resistance. On the function curve graph, the operating point lies at the intersection of the cardiac and vascular function curves. Exercise increases inotropy, shifting the cardiac function curve upward, and decreases TPR, which rotates the vascular function curve so that more venous return occurs at a given right atrial pressure. These changes occur in tandem and are reinforcing, maximizing cardiac output. In heart failure, in contrast, decreased inotropy is compensated by fluid retention to increase preload.

B.reason: Decreased inotropy and increased TPR would lower cardiac output, as in heart failure or with vasopressors. They would not allow a fivefold rise in output.

C.reason: Increased inotropy would raise the cardiac function curve, but increased TPR would reduce venous return and limit output. His measured TPR is markedly lower.
