correct_explanation: An aorta arising from the right ventricle and a pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle define D-transposition of the great arteries, which creates parallel systemic and pulmonary circulations. The cause is failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral, and the narrow superior mediastinum produces the egg-on-a-string appearance. It is not compatible with life unless a shunt is present to allow mixing of blood, such as a VSD, PDA, or patent foramen ovale. Without surgery most infants die within the first few months of life. Maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandins preserves mixing until repair.

B.reason: Closing the ductus would eliminate a key mixing site and could be fatal. Ductal patency is maintained with prostaglandin E1 in this condition.

C.reason: Pulmonary stenosis is a feature of tetralogy of Fallot, not a survival mechanism in TGA. It would restrict pulmonary blood flow further.

D.reason: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance would favor right-to-left flow and does not help mix blood in a parallel circulation. It is characteristic of PPHN.

E.reason: Absence of the foramen ovale would eliminate an atrial mixing site, worsening the infant's condition. A patent foramen ovale is one of the shunts that permits survival.

high_yield_pearl: D-TGA is not compatible with life unless a VSD, PDA, or PFO allows blood to mix.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Aorta leaves the RV (anterior) and pulmonary trunk leaves the LV (posterior), separating systemic and pulmonary circulations; due to failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral.
-  Clinical Findings: Early cyanosis; egg-on-a-string appearance on CXR; associated with maternal diabetes.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
-  Management: Maintain PDA with prostaglandins and surgical repair; most infants die within months without surgery.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with a known dilated cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 28% presents with worsening exertional dyspnea. Her heart rate is 94/min and blood pressure is 106/68 mm Hg. A high-pitched holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex and radiates toward the axilla, and S2 is normal. She has no history of rheumatic fever, MI, or endocarditis, and echocardiography shows a structurally normal mitral valve with a dilated annulus. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her regurgitation?
option_A: Left ventricular dilatation
option_C: Chordae tendineae rupture from myxomatous degeneration
correct_explanation: A high-pitched holosystolic murmur loudest at the apex and radiating toward the axilla is mitral regurgitation. MR is often due to ischemic heart disease (post-MI), MVP, LV dilatation, or rheumatic fever, and infective endocarditis is another cause. In this patient, the valve is structurally normal, and the annulus is dilated in the setting of a dilated left ventricle. The enlarged ventricle displaces the papillary muscles and stretches the annulus, preventing the leaflets from coapting, a functional MR. The absence of rheumatic, ischemic, and infectious history excludes the other causes.

B.reason: Rheumatic fever is a recognized cause of MR but causes structural leaflet and chordal changes and she has no history. Her valve is structurally normal.

C.reason: Chordae rupture from myxomatous degeneration causes MVP and MR with a midsystolic click and a structurally abnormal valve. Her valve is normal.

D.reason: Ischemic papillary muscle rupture is an acute complication 2–7 days after MI and causes acute pulmonary edema. She has no MI and a chronic presentation.

E.reason: Infective endocarditis causes MR with vegetations and fever. She has neither and a normal valve on echocardiography.

high_yield_pearl: Functional MR arises from LV dilatation; other causes: post-MI ischemia, MVP, rheumatic fever, endocarditis.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: MR: holosystolic, high-pitched blowing murmur loudest at the apex, radiating toward the axilla; often due to ischemic heart disease (post-MI), MVP, LV dilatation, or rheumatic fever; infective endocarditis can cause MR or TR.
-  Clinical Findings: Dyspnea; holosystolic murmur.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
-  Management: Treat the underlying cause; valve repair or replacement when indicated.

concept_name: Septation of the atria: formation of the ostium secundum
stem: A 20-week fetal echocardiogram in a healthy pregnancy shows an opening within the septum primum, with blood passing from the right to the left atrium. The ostium primum is no longer visible, and a thick muscular crescent is forming to the right of the septum primum. The obstetric cardiologist reassures the parents that this is a normal stage. Which of the following processes creates the opening in the septum primum?
option_A: Cell death within the septum primum
option_D: Fusion of septum primum with septum secundum after birth
option_E: Migration of neural crest cells into the outflow tract
correct_explanation: The septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions and narrows the ostium primum, which then regresses. The ostium secundum forms in the septum primum due to cell death, so that right-to-left shunting is maintained in fetal life. The septum secundum develops to the right of the septum primum and covers most of the ostium secundum, with the residual foramen being the foramen ovale. The remaining portion of the septum primum forms the one-way valve of the foramen ovale. After birth, the septa fuse, and failure to fuse leaves a PFO.

B.reason: Endocardial cushion growth separates the atria from the ventricles and contributes to septation, but it does not create the ostium secundum. Cushion defects cause AV septal defects.

C.reason: Rotation of the aorticopulmonary septum fuses with the muscular septum to form the membranous interventricular septum. It is a ventricular and outflow process.

D.reason: Fusion of the septa occurs after birth in infancy or early childhood, closing the foramen ovale. It does not create the opening.

E.reason: Neural crest migration forms the truncal and bulbar ridges of the outflow tract. It does not participate in atrial septation.

high_yield_pearl: The ostium secundum forms in the septum primum by cell death, maintaining the fetal right-to-left shunt.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Atrial septation: septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions, narrowing the ostium primum; the ostium secundum forms in the septum primum by cell death (the ostium primum regresses); septum secundum develops to the right and covers most of the ostium secundum; the residual foramen is the foramen ovale; the remaining septum primum forms the one-way valve.
-  Clinical Findings: Failure of fusion leaves a PFO (25% of the population).
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
-  Management: Usually none.

concept_name: Hypertension: obstructive sleep apnea as a secondary cause
stem: A 48-year-old man with a BMI of 38 kg/m2 has resistant hypertension despite three antihypertensive drugs, with an office blood pressure of 164/102 mm Hg. His wife reports loud snoring with witnessed apneas, and he has morning headaches and falls asleep during meetings. Serum potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, plasma renin and aldosterone are normal, and renal artery duplex ultrasonography shows normal flow. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypertension?
option_A: Obstructive sleep apnea
correct_explanation: Resistant hypertension with obesity, snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headaches, and daytime sleepiness points to obstructive sleep apnea as a secondary cause. About 90% of hypertension is primary, and the remaining 10% is mostly secondary to renal or renovascular disease, primary hyperaldosteronism, or obstructive sleep apnea. Recurrent apneas increase sympathetic tone, which raises blood pressure and increases the pulse pressure. His normal potassium, renin, and aldosterone levels and normal renal artery flow exclude the other causes. Treatment of the sleep apnea can improve blood pressure control.

B.reason: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes a string-of-beads renal artery in young women. This man's renal duplex is normal.

C.reason: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension with hypokalemia and suppressed renin. His potassium and aldosterone are normal.

D.reason: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis would be seen on renal duplex and typically affects older patients with vascular disease. His renal arteries are normal.

E.reason: Coarctation causes upper-extremity hypertension with delayed femoral pulses, and presents earlier. His presentation lacks pulse deficits.

high_yield_pearl: Resistant hypertension plus snoring and daytime sleepiness suggests obstructive sleep apnea.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: 90% of hypertension is primary (essential), related to increased CO or TPR; the remaining 10% is mostly secondary to renal or renovascular disease (fibromuscular dysplasia, atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis), primary hyperaldosteronism, or obstructive sleep apnea.
-  Clinical Findings: OSA increases sympathetic tone and pulse pressure.
-  Diagnostics: Polysomnography; screen for other secondary causes.
-  Management: Treat OSA and hypertension.

stem: A 61-year-old man with coronary artery disease has taken simvastatin for 3 years. Two weeks ago, gemfibrozil was added for hypertriglyceridemia. He now has severe diffuse muscle pain and weakness, and his urine is dark brown. Creatine kinase is 12,400 U/L, creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL, and urinalysis is positive for blood on dipstick with no red cells on microscopy. Which of the following best explains his condition?
option_A: Statin-associated myopathy potentiated by the fibrate
correct_explanation: Diffuse myalgias and weakness with a markedly elevated creatine kinase, dark urine, and renal impairment indicate rhabdomyolysis, a severe form of statin myopathy. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and cause adverse effects such as hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs) and myopathy, especially when used with fibrates or niacin. Fibrates such as gemfibrozil also carry a risk of myopathy when combined with statins. The temporal association with adding gemfibrozil to simvastatin makes this combination the likely cause. The dipstick positive for blood without red cells reflects myoglobinuria.

B.reason: Niacin causes prostaglandin-mediated flushing, hyperglycemia, and hyperuricemia. He is not taking niacin, and flushing does not explain a CK of 12,400.

C.reason: Cholesterol gallstones are an adverse effect of fibrates through inhibition of cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase and present with biliary colic. They do not produce myoglobinuria.

D.reason: Bile acid resins cause GI upset and reduced absorption of drugs and fat-soluble vitamins. He is not taking a resin and has muscle injury.

E.reason: PCSK9 inhibitors have minimal drug interactions and are not hepatotoxic in this way. He is not taking one.

high_yield_pearl: Statin plus fibrate (or niacin) raises the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, decreasing intrahepatic cholesterol and increasing LDL receptor recycling and LDL catabolism; decrease mortality in CAD.
-  Clinical Findings: Adverse effects: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), myopathy (especially with fibrates or niacin). Fibrates also cause cholesterol gallstones.
-  Diagnostics: CK, creatinine, urinalysis; LFTs.
-  Management: Stop the offending drugs and give supportive care for rhabdomyolysis.

stem: A 42-year-old man with a known bicuspid aortic valve reports exertional dyspnea and a pounding sensation in his chest. Blood pressure is 164/42 mm Hg and heart rate is 76/min. His head nods with each heartbeat, and a high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with a regurgitant jet filling the outflow tract. Which of the following best explains his widened pulse pressure?
option_A: Increased stroke volume with rapid diastolic runoff of blood back into the left ventricle
option_B: Decreased stroke volume with delayed ejection
option_C: Increased total peripheral resistance with decreased aortic compliance only
correct_explanation: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur with head bobbing and a wide pulse pressure in a patient with a bicuspid valve indicates chronic aortic regurgitation (the causes spell BEAR: bicuspid valve, endocarditis, aortic root dilation, rheumatic fever). In AR, blood leaks back into the left ventricle during diastole, so the LV receives both the normal inflow and the regurgitant volume. The larger end-diastolic volume produces a larger stroke volume and a higher systolic pressure. The regurgitant runoff during diastole lowers the diastolic pressure. Pulse pressure is directly proportional to stroke volume, so it widens, producing a hyperdynamic pulse, pistol-shot femoral pulse, pulsing nail beds, and head bobbing.

B.reason: A decreased stroke volume narrows the pulse pressure, as in aortic stenosis, tamponade, and cardiogenic shock. This patient's stroke volume is increased.

C.reason: Decreased compliance can widen the pulse pressure in older adults but does not explain the very low diastolic pressure with a diastolic murmur in a young patient. The regurgitant lesion is the cause.

D.reason: A decreased blood volume would lower stroke volume and narrow the pulse pressure. It would not produce a widened pulse pressure or a diastolic murmur.

E.reason: Impaired left atrial emptying describes mitral stenosis, with a diastolic rumble and opening snap and a narrow pulse pressure. This patient has a decrescendo diastolic murmur and a wide pulse pressure.

high_yield_pearl: AR: early diastolic decrescendo murmur, wide pulse pressure, and bounding pulses (BEAR causes).
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: AR: early diastolic, decrescendo, high-pitched blowing murmur best heard at the base (aortic root dilation) or left sternal border (valvular disease); causes include BEAR: Bicuspid valve, Endocarditis, Aortic root dilation, Rheumatic fever.
-  Clinical Findings: Wide pulse pressure, pistol-shot femoral pulse, pulsing nail bed, hyperdynamic pulse, and head bobbing when severe and chronic.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
-  Management: Can progress to left HF; valve replacement when indicated.

concept_name: Heart murmurs: mitral stenosis and the opening snap
stem: A 44-year-old woman born in a region with limited access to penicillin has had progressive exertional dyspnea and two episodes of hemoptysis. Heart rate is 88/min and irregularly irregular, and ECG shows atrial fibrillation. A high-pitched sound is heard shortly after S2 at the apex, followed by a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur. Echocardiography shows thickened mitral leaflets with fusion at the tips and doming in diastole. Which of the following best explains the sound heard just after S2?
option_A: Abrupt halt of leaflet motion in diastole after rapid opening due to fusion at the leaflet tips
option_B: Rapid filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle
option_C: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
option_D: Sudden tensing of chordae tendineae as leaflets prolapse
option_E: Early systolic halt of a stenotic aortic valve
correct_explanation: A diastolic rumble preceded by a high-pitched sound after S2, hemoptysis, atrial fibrillation, and a doming, fused mitral valve indicate mitral stenosis due to rheumatic heart disease, a late and highly specific sequela of rheumatic fever. The opening snap occurs because the leaflets, fused at the tips, open rapidly in diastole under high left atrial pressure and then halt abruptly, producing the sound. The LA pressure exceeds the LV pressure throughout diastole, producing the rumbling murmur. Chronic MS can lead to LA dilation, pulmonary congestion, atrial fibrillation, Ortner syndrome, hemoptysis, and right heart failure. The S2-OS interval shortens as stenosis becomes more severe.

B.reason: Rapid filling of a dilated ventricle produces an S3, which occurs in early diastole in heart failure or regurgitant lesions. The opening snap here is explained by leaflet fusion.

C.reason: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle produces an S4, a late diastolic sound that is absent in atrial fibrillation. This patient's sound follows S2 closely.

D.reason: Sudden tensing of chordae tendineae produces the midsystolic click of mitral valve prolapse, which is a systolic sound.

E.reason: An early systolic halt of a stenotic aortic valve produces an ejection click, which is a systolic sound at the base. This patient's sound is diastolic.

high_yield_pearl: The opening snap is the abrupt halt of fused mitral leaflets after rapid opening in diastole.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: MS follows rheumatic fever (late, highly specific sequela); OS is due to abrupt halt in leaflet motion in diastole after rapid opening due to fusion at the leaflet tips; LA pressure exceeds LV pressure during diastole.
-  Clinical Findings: Delayed rumbling mid-to-late diastolic murmur after the OS; decreased S2-OS interval correlates with increased severity; chronic MS can result in LA dilation, pulmonary congestion, AF, Ortner syndrome, hemoptysis, right HF.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
-  Management: Rate control, anticoagulation for AF, valve intervention.

stem: A 78-year-old man with exertional presyncope has a harsh systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids. His carotid upstroke is delayed and S2 is soft. During auscultation at the left upper sternal border, two components of S2 are heard on expiration, and they fuse into a single sound on inspiration. Which of the following best explains this finding?
option_A: Delayed aortic valve closure causes P2 to precede A2, and inspiration delays P2 so that it merges with A2
option_B: Delayed pulmonic valve closure with exaggerated inspiratory splitting
option_C: Fixed delay of P2 independent of respiration
option_D: Premature closure of the aortic valve
option_E: Normal physiologic delay of P2 on inspiration
correct_explanation: Presyncope, a systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, a delayed carotid upstroke, and a soft S2 indicate aortic stenosis. Conditions that delay aortic valve closure, such as aortic stenosis and left bundle branch block, produce paradoxical splitting. The normal order of semilunar valve closure is reversed, so P2 occurs before A2. On inspiration, P2 closes later and moves closer to A2, paradoxically eliminating the split, while on expiration the split can be heard, which is the opposite of physiologic splitting. This explains the patient's findings.

B.reason: Delayed pulmonic closure produces wide splitting, which is heard on inspiration and narrows on expiration. This patient's split is heard on expiration and disappears on inspiration.

C.reason: A fixed delay independent of respiration occurs with ASD. This patient's split varies with respiration, and he has aortic stenosis.

D.reason: Premature closure of the aortic valve would produce a wide split with A2 early, which would widen on inspiration. The patient's aortic valve closes late.

E.reason: Physiologic splitting is heard on inspiration and absent on expiration. This patient shows the opposite pattern.

high_yield_pearl: Paradoxical split: delayed A2 (aortic stenosis, LBBB) so the split is heard on expiration.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Paradoxical splitting occurs in conditions that delay aortic valve closure (aortic stenosis, LBBB); P2 precedes A2; inspiration delays P2 toward A2 and eliminates the split; the split is heard on expiration.
-  Clinical Findings: Compare physiologic (inspiration split), wide (pulmonic stenosis, RBBB), and fixed (ASD) splitting.
-  Diagnostics: Auscultation across the respiratory cycle.
-  Management: Treat the underlying lesion.

concept_name: Pressure-volume loops: aortic stenosis and ventricular hypertrophy
stem: A 69-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis undergoes cardiac catheterization. Left ventricular pressure-volume analysis shows an increased peak systolic pressure, an increased end-systolic volume, and a decreased stroke volume. At a given end-diastolic volume, his end-diastolic pressure is markedly higher than normal. Which of the following best explains the elevated end-diastolic pressure?
option_A: Ventricular hypertrophy decreasing ventricular compliance
option_B: Impaired ventricular filling from mitral stenosis
option_C: Regurgitation into the left atrium during systole
option_E: Increased venous return from AV shunting
correct_explanation: In aortic stenosis, the left ventricle must generate a higher pressure to eject through the narrowed valve, so the pressure-volume loop shows increased LV pressure, increased end-systolic volume, decreased stroke volume, and no change in end-diastolic volume if the disease is mild. The chronic pressure load produces concentric hypertrophy, and the thick ventricle has decreased compliance. Reduced compliance means that for a given end-diastolic volume, the end-diastolic pressure is higher. This stiffness underlies the S4 and the diastolic dysfunction in aortic stenosis. The other lesions listed would produce different loop patterns.

B.reason: Mitral stenosis impairs ventricular filling and decreases EDV, ESV, and SV, with an increased LA pressure. This patient has a pressure-loaded left ventricle with an elevated peak pressure.

C.reason: Regurgitation into the left atrium in mitral regurgitation lowers ESV and raises EDV and SV, and removes the true isovolumetric phases. This patient's ESV is increased and SV is decreased.

D.reason: The isovolumetric phases are lost in regurgitant lesions (AR and MR), not in aortic stenosis, in which they remain. Their loss would not explain the increased end-diastolic pressure.

E.reason: Increased venous return from AV shunting raises preload and produces high-output HF with decreased SVR. It does not match the loop of aortic stenosis.

high_yield_pearl: Aortic stenosis loop: high LV pressure, high ESV, low SV, and hypertrophy-related increase in end-diastolic pressure.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Aortic stenosis: increased LV pressure, increased ESV, no change in EDV (if mild), decreased SV; ventricular hypertrophy decreases ventricular compliance, increasing EDP for a given EDV.
-  Clinical Findings: Crescendo-decrescendo murmur, S4 from the stiff ventricle.
-  Diagnostics: Pressure-volume loop analysis, echocardiography.
-  Management: Valve replacement when symptomatic.

stem: A 61-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer presents with worsening dyspnea and lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 82/58 mm Hg and heart rate is 124/min, and his neck veins are distended with distant heart sounds. ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes with beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude. Echocardiography shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with systolic right atrial collapse and diastolic right ventricular collapse. Which of the following hemodynamic findings is expected on catheterization?
option_A: Equilibration of diastolic pressures in all four cardiac chambers
option_B: Markedly elevated left atrial pressure with normal right-sided pressures
option_C: A step-up in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle
option_D: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with low central venous pressure
option_E: A large systolic gradient across the aortic valve
correct_explanation: Hypotension, tachycardia, distended neck veins, distant heart sounds, low-voltage QRS with electrical alternans, and an effusion with chamber collapse indicate cardiac tamponade (Beck triad plus pulsus paradoxus). Compression of the heart by fluid, such as blood or an effusion, decreases cardiac output. The pericardial pressure rises until diastolic pressures in all four chambers are equilibrated. Electrical alternans is due to the swinging movement of the heart in a large effusion, and echocardiography shows systolic RA collapse, diastolic RV collapse, and IVC plethora. Treatment is pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage.

B.reason: A markedly elevated LA pressure with normal right pressures suggests isolated left-sided disease such as mitral stenosis. Tamponade equalizes pressures in all chambers.

C.reason: A step-up in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle indicates a VSD, as after septal rupture. This patient has an effusion with no shunt.

D.reason: A high wedge with a low central venous pressure is inconsistent with tamponade, in which venous pressure is elevated and the neck veins are distended.

E.reason: A large aortic valve systolic gradient indicates aortic stenosis. This patient has no murmur and a pericardial effusion.

high_yield_pearl: Tamponade: Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans, and equalized diastolic pressures.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Compression of the heart by fluid (blood, effusion) decreases CO; equilibration of diastolic pressures in all four chambers.
-  Clinical Findings: Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, distant heart sounds), increased HR, pulsus paradoxus; ECG low-voltage QRS and/or electrical alternans.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography: pericardial effusion, systolic RA collapse, diastolic RV collapse, IVC plethora.
-  Management: Pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage.

stem: A 26-year-old woman develops hives, wheezing, and lightheadedness 10 minutes after eating a peanut-containing dessert. Blood pressure is 68/32 mm Hg and heart rate is 142/min, and her skin is warm, flushed, and dry. She is given intramuscular epinephrine. Before treatment, invasive monitoring in the emergency department shows hemodynamic abnormalities. Which of the following hemodynamic profiles is expected?
option_A: Decreased CVP, decreased PCWP, increased CO, decreased SVR
option_B: Increased CVP, increased PCWP, decreased CO, increased SVR
option_C: Decreased CVP, decreased PCWP, decreased CO, increased SVR
option_D: Increased CVP, decreased PCWP, decreased CO, increased SVR
option_E: Increased CVP, increased PCWP, increased CO, decreased SVR
correct_explanation: Hives, wheezing, and hypotension minutes after allergen exposure indicate anaphylaxis, which causes distributive shock through systemic vasodilation. Warm, dry skin early reflects peripheral vasodilation. The hemodynamic profile of distributive shock is decreased CVP and PCWP from pooling of blood, decreased SVR from vasodilation, and increased cardiac output as the heart compensates. Mixed venous oxygen saturation tends to be increased as tissues extract less oxygen. Other types of distributive shock include early sepsis and CNS injury.

B.reason: Increased CVP and PCWP with decreased CO and increased SVR is the profile of cardiogenic shock from left heart dysfunction. This patient has warm skin and vasodilation.

C.reason: Decreased filling pressures with decreased CO and increased SVR is the profile of hypovolemic shock with cold, clammy skin. This patient is warm and vasodilated.

D.reason: Increased CVP with decreased PCWP and CO suggests obstructive shock such as pulmonary embolism. This patient has an allergic trigger and warm skin.

E.reason: Increased filling pressures with a decreased SVR does not describe distributive shock, in which filling pressures are low. It would not fit anaphylaxis.

high_yield_pearl: Distributive shock: warm skin, low SVR, low filling pressures, and high CO.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Distributive shock (sepsis early, anaphylaxis, CNS injury): systemic vasodilation; warm, dry skin.
-  Clinical Findings: CVP decreased, PCWP decreased, CO increased, SVR decreased, SvO2 increased.
-  Diagnostics: Hemodynamic profile.
-  Management: Treat the cause; epinephrine for anaphylaxis.

stem: A 66-year-old man with long-standing hypertension presents with abrupt tearing interscapular pain. Blood pressure is 188/100 mm Hg in both arms and heart rate is 96/min, with no murmur and intact peripheral pulses. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum, and CT angiography shows an intimal flap beginning distal to the left subclavian artery with no involvement of the ascending aorta or arch. He has no signs of organ ischemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
option_A: Intravenous beta-blocker followed by vasodilators
option_B: Emergent surgical repair of the ascending aorta
correct_explanation: Tearing pain with a widened mediastinum and a flap beginning distal to the left subclavian artery indicates a Stanford type B aortic dissection involving only the descending aorta. Hypertension is the strongest risk factor, as in this patient. Type B dissection is treated medically with beta-blockers first, then vasodilators, to reduce shear stress and blood pressure. The beta-blocker should precede the vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia, which would increase aortic wall stress. Type A dissection, in contrast, involves the ascending aorta and requires surgery.

B.reason: Emergent surgery is indicated for type A dissection, which can cause aortic regurgitation, tamponade, and rupture. This patient has an uncomplicated type B dissection.

C.reason: Fibrinolysis could cause catastrophic bleeding into the false lumen and is used for STEMI when PCI is unavailable. This patient has an aortic dissection.

D.reason: Heparin is used in ACS and DVT, and anticoagulation in aortic dissection risks hemorrhage and extension of the false lumen.

E.reason: Observation without blood pressure control risks propagation and rupture. Hypertension must be treated promptly.

high_yield_pearl: Type B dissection (below the left subclavian): beta-blockers first, then vasodilators.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Longitudinal intimal tear forming a false lumen; hypertension is the strongest risk factor; also bicuspid valve and connective tissue disorders. Stanford type B involves only the descending aorta below the left subclavian artery.
-  Clinical Findings: Tearing sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the back; unequal arm BP in some; mediastinal widening.
-  Diagnostics: CT angiography.
-  Management: Type B: beta-blockers, then vasodilators; type A: surgery.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension has progressive proteinuria and a creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL. Renal biopsy shows glomerulosclerosis, and the afferent arterioles have thickened walls with a homogeneous, pink, glassy appearance and narrowed lumens. There is no concentric laminated proliferation of smooth muscle cells. Which of the following best explains the arteriolar change?
option_A: Plasma protein leak into the subendothelium
option_B: Proliferation of smooth muscle cells with onion skinning
option_C: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
correct_explanation: Homogeneous pink thickening of renal arteriolar walls in a patient with long-standing diabetes and hypertension is hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Arteriolosclerosis affects small arteries and arterioles and has two types. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is vessel wall thickening secondary to plasma protein leak into the subendothelium in hypertension or diabetes mellitus. Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, by contrast, shows onion skinning from smooth muscle proliferation in severe hypertension. The narrowed lumens reduce renal perfusion and contribute to progressive nephron loss.

B.reason: Onion skinning from smooth muscle proliferation defines hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis in severe hypertension. This biopsy lacks laminated proliferation.

C.reason: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum occurs in tertiary syphilis and affects the aorta. It is not a renal arteriolar change.

D.reason: Cystic medial degeneration affects the aortic media in Marfan syndrome and hypertension and is not an arteriolar change.

E.reason: Cholesterol embolization causes cholesterol clefts in small arteries after vascular procedures, not homogeneous thickening of arteriolar walls.

high_yield_pearl: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis: protein leak into the arteriolar wall in diabetes and hypertension.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Arteriolosclerosis affects small arteries and arterioles; hyaline type: wall thickening secondary to plasma protein leak into the subendothelium in hypertension or diabetes.
-  Clinical Findings: Nephrosclerosis, proteinuria, declining renal function.
-  Diagnostics: Renal biopsy.
-  Management: Control blood pressure and glucose; ACEi or ARB protect against diabetic nephropathy.

stem: A 55-year-old woman is admitted with a thunderclap headache, and CT shows subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm, which is secured on hospital day 1. Her blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg and she is alert and neurologically intact. The neurointensivist starts an oral medication to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
option_A: Nimodipine
correct_explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage carries a risk of delayed cerebral ischemia from cerebral vasospasm several days after the bleed. Nimodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that acts on vascular smooth muscle and is used in subarachnoid hemorrhage to prevent delayed ischemia. Dihydropyridines other than nimodipine are used for hypertension, angina (including vasospastic), and Raynaud phenomenon. Nicardipine and clevidipine are used for hypertensive urgency or emergency. Nimodipine's role is unique among the group.

B.reason: Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine acting mainly on the heart, used for rate control in atrial fibrillation and prevention of nodal arrhythmias. It is not indicated to prevent vasospasm after SAH.

C.reason: Hydralazine is an arteriolar vasodilator for severe hypertension and pregnancy and has no neuroprotective role in SAH. It could cause reflex tachycardia.

D.reason: Nitroprusside treats hypertensive emergency and can raise intracranial pressure as a vasodilator, with a risk of cyanide toxicity. It is not used to prevent delayed ischemia.

E.reason: Labetalol is used for hypertensive emergency and pregnancy hypertension, but it does not prevent vasospasm-related ischemia.

high_yield_pearl: Nimodipine prevents delayed cerebral ischemia after subarachnoid hemorrhage.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Calcium channel blockers block voltage-dependent L-type Ca2+ channels of cardiac and smooth muscle, decreasing contractility; dihydropyridines (amlodipine, clevidipine, nicardipine, nifedipine, nimodipine) act on vascular smooth muscle.
-  Clinical Findings: Nimodipine: subarachnoid hemorrhage (prevents delayed ischemia); other dihydropyridines: hypertension, angina (including vasospastic), Raynaud phenomenon; nicardipine and clevidipine: hypertensive urgency or emergency.
-  Diagnostics: Neurologic monitoring.
-  Management: Adverse effects: gingival hyperplasia, peripheral edema, flushing, dizziness.

stem: A 34-year-old woman reports that her fingers turn white, then blue, then red when she is exposed to cold or stress, with numbness and throbbing on rewarming. Her symptoms have worsened over 2 years, and she has no skin thickening, joint pain, or digital ulcers. Blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg, and nailfold capillaroscopy and antinuclear antibodies are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug therapy if lifestyle measures fail?
option_A: Nifedipine
correct_explanation: Episodic digital pallor, cyanosis, and redness with cold and stress in a patient with normal autoimmune testing is primary Raynaud phenomenon, caused by exaggerated vasospasm of digital arteries. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine and amlodipine are the drugs of choice because they block L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and dilate arteries. First Aid lists Raynaud phenomenon among the uses of dihydropyridines. Nondihydropyridines act mainly on the heart and are not first choice. Beta-blockers can worsen peripheral vasospasm.

B.reason: Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker that blocks vasodilatory beta-2 receptors and can worsen vasospasm. It is not used for Raynaud phenomenon.

C.reason: Verapamil acts mainly on the heart and has less vascular selectivity, so it is less effective for arterial vasospasm and carries risks of AV block and constipation.

D.reason: Hydralazine is an arteriolar vasodilator used for severe hypertension and in pregnancy and is not recommended for Raynaud phenomenon. It can cause reflex tachycardia and drug-induced lupus.

E.reason: Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective blocker that can reduce peripheral blood flow and does not treat vasospasm.

high_yield_pearl: Dihydropyridine CCBs (nifedipine, amlodipine) treat Raynaud phenomenon.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Dihydropyridines block L-type Ca2+ channels in vascular smooth muscle, dilating arteries.
-  Clinical Findings: Uses: hypertension, angina (including vasospastic), Raynaud phenomenon; adverse effects: peripheral edema, flushing, dizziness, gingival hyperplasia.
-  Diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis; exclude secondary causes.
-  Management: Dihydropyridine CCB when cold avoidance fails.

stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 8 years has a blood pressure of 148/92 mm Hg on repeated visits. His urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 180 mg/g and his eGFR is 78 mL/min, with a normal potassium. He has no asthma, gout, or history of angioedema. His physician wants an antihypertensive that also protects the kidney. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial drug?
option_A: Lisinopril
correct_explanation: Hypertension with diabetes and albuminuria requires an agent with renal protective effects. In patients with diabetes, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and beta-blockers are all options, but ACE inhibitors and ARBs are protective against diabetic nephropathy. Beta-blockers can mask the symptoms of hypoglycemia, which is a drawback in a patient with diabetes. Lisinopril is therefore the best initial choice. It also decreases preload and afterload.

B.reason: Atenolol is a beta-blocker that can mask hypoglycemia symptoms and provides no renal protection, so it is not the best first choice in this patient.

C.reason: Hydrochlorothiazide lowers blood pressure and is acceptable in diabetes but does not protect against diabetic nephropathy and can raise glucose and uric acid.

D.reason: Hydralazine is reserved for severe or acute hypertension and pregnancy, and it causes reflex tachycardia. It does not protect the kidney.

E.reason: Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine CCB used for rate control and can cause constipation and AV block. It provides no specific renal protection.

high_yield_pearl: Hypertension with diabetes: ACE inhibitors or ARBs protect against diabetic nephropathy.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: ACE inhibitors and ARBs protect against diabetic nephropathy; beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia symptoms.
-  Clinical Findings: Diabetic hypertension with albuminuria.
-  Diagnostics: Urine albumin, eGFR, potassium.
-  Management: ACEi or ARB, Ca2+ channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers as options.

stem: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis and a prior vertebral compression fracture has newly diagnosed stage 2 hypertension with a blood pressure of 154/94 mm Hg. Serum calcium is 9.4 mg/dL and potassium is 4.3 mEq/L, and she has no history of gout or kidney stones. Her physician selects a monotherapy agent that may also support bone health. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice and mechanism?
option_A: Hydrochlorothiazide, which increases renal calcium reabsorption
option_B: Furosemide, which increases renal calcium excretion
option_C: Amlodipine, which blocks vascular calcium channels
correct_explanation: In a patient with osteoporosis and hypertension, thiazide diuretics are preferred as monotherapy and can be combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs if needed. Thiazides are preferred because of increased calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, which reduces urinary calcium loss and favors bone density. Loop diuretics have the opposite effect, increasing calcium excretion. Hydrochlorothiazide is therefore the best choice for this patient, provided she has no gout or hypercalcemia.

B.reason: Furosemide increases urinary calcium excretion and could worsen osteoporosis. It is not preferred in this patient.

C.reason: Amlodipine is an acceptable antihypertensive but has no effect on calcium handling in bone. It does not provide the added bone benefit of a thiazide.

D.reason: Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker with no bone benefit and several adverse effects. It is not preferred here.

E.reason: Hydralazine is used for severe or acute hypertension and pregnancy and has no effect on calcium reabsorption. It would also cause reflex tachycardia.

high_yield_pearl: Hypertension with osteoporosis: thiazides, because they increase calcium reabsorption.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Thiazides increase renal Ca2+ reabsorption; preferred as monotherapy in hypertension with osteoporosis; combine with ACE inhibitors or ARBs if needed.
-  Clinical Findings: Postmenopausal osteoporosis with hypertension.
-  Diagnostics: Serum calcium and potassium.
-  Management: Thiazide first; avoid in gout and hypercalcemia.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 6 weeks pregnant by dates undergoes transvaginal ultrasonography for spotting. The scan shows a single embryo with a flickering cardiac activity at 110/min. The sonographer comments that the heart is the first functional organ in the embryo. Which of the following best describes the status of the embryonic heart at this stage?
option_A: A primary heart tube that has begun looping to establish left-right polarity and is beating spontaneously
option_B: A fully septated four-chambered heart with functioning valves
option_C: A heart with completed aorticopulmonary septation and closed foramen ovale
option_D: A heart that has not yet begun to contract
option_E: A heart in which fetal-postnatal remnants have already formed
correct_explanation: The heart is the first functional organ in vertebrate embryos and beats spontaneously by 4–5 weeks of development. At this stage, the primary heart tube loops, a process that begins in week 4 and establishes left-right polarity. Septation of the atria, ventricles, and outflow tract occurs later and is not complete at 6 weeks. A defect in left-right dynein during looping can lead to dextrocardia, as in Kartagener syndrome. Fetal-postnatal remnants such as the ligamentum arteriosum form only after birth.

B.reason: A fully septated four-chambered heart with functioning valves is not present at 6 weeks, since septation occurs later. At this stage the embryonic heart is still looping and developing septa.

C.reason: Aorticopulmonary septation and the later fusion with the muscular septum are not complete at 6 weeks, and the foramen ovale remains open throughout fetal life.

D.reason: The heart begins beating spontaneously by 4–5 weeks, so cardiac activity is expected at 6 weeks. Absent activity would suggest a failing pregnancy.

E.reason: Fetal-postnatal derivatives such as the ligamentum arteriosum and fossa ovalis form after birth, not during embryonic development.

high_yield_pearl: The heart beats by weeks 4–5 and loops in week 4 to set left-right polarity.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Heart is the first functional organ in vertebrate embryos and beats spontaneously by 4–5 weeks; the primary heart tube loops to establish left-right polarity beginning in week 4.
-  Clinical Findings: A left-right dynein defect can cause dextrocardia (Kartagener syndrome).
-  Diagnostics: Transvaginal ultrasonography shows cardiac activity.
-  Management: Not applicable.

concept_name: Heart embryology: right horn of the sinus venosus
stem: A 17-year-old boy undergoes electrophysiologic mapping for recurrent supraventricular tachycardia. The cardiologist notes that the posterior wall of the right atrium where the venae cavae enter is smooth, whereas the right atrial appendage has prominent muscular ridges. The ablation target lies in the smooth-walled portion. Which of the following embryonic structures gives rise to the smooth-walled part of the right atrium?
option_A: Right horn of the sinus venosus
option_C: Left horn of the sinus venosus
correct_explanation: The right atrium has a smooth part, the sinus venarum, where the venae cavae enter, and a trabeculated part that includes the appendage. The right horn of the sinus venosus gives rise to the smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum). The primitive atrium forms the trabeculated parts of both the left and right atria. The left horn of the sinus venosus forms the coronary sinus, and the primitive pulmonary vein forms the smooth part of the left atrium. This distinction explains why the two regions of the right atrium look different.

B.reason: The primitive atrium forms the trabeculated parts of the left and right atria, including the right atrial appendage. The question concerns the smooth portion.

C.reason: The left horn of the sinus venosus forms the coronary sinus, not part of the right atrial wall.

D.reason: The primitive pulmonary vein forms the smooth part of the left atrium, where the pulmonary veins enter.

E.reason: The bulbus cordis forms the smooth outflow portions of the ventricles, not part of the atrium.

high_yield_pearl: Right sinus horn gives the smooth right atrium (sinus venarum); the primitive atrium gives the trabeculated parts.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Right horn of sinus venosus: smooth part of RA (sinus venarum); left horn: coronary sinus; primitive pulmonary vein: smooth part of LA; primitive atrium: trabeculated parts of LA and RA.
-  Clinical Findings: Developmental anatomy guides electrophysiology mapping.
-  Diagnostics: Imaging and electrophysiologic mapping.
-  Management: Not applicable.

stem: A fetal echocardiographer evaluates a 22-week fetus with a family history of congenital valve disease. She notes that the aortic and pulmonary valves appear to develop from one source and the mitral and tricuspid valves from another. A newborn with severe mitral and tricuspid valve anomalies is later evaluated by a pathologist who reviews the embryology. Which of the following structures give rise to the mitral and tricuspid valves?
option_A: Fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal
option_B: Endocardial cushions of the outflow tract
correct_explanation: The mitral and tricuspid valves are derived from the fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal. In contrast, the aortic and pulmonary valves are derived from the endocardial cushions of the outflow tract. Valvular anomalies may be stenotic, regurgitant, atretic (eg, tricuspid atresia), or displaced (eg, Ebstein anomaly). The same AV canal cushions contribute to the atrial septum and membranous interventricular septum, so cushion defects can affect both septa and valves.

B.reason: The endocardial cushions of the outflow tract form the aortic and pulmonary valves, not the AV valves.

C.reason: The septum primum forms the one-way flap of the foramen ovale and part of the atrial septum. It does not form the AV valves.

D.reason: The truncus arteriosus forms the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, not the valves of the AV canal.

E.reason: The bulbus cordis forms the smooth outflow tracts of the ventricles and not the mitral and tricuspid valves.

high_yield_pearl: Mitral and tricuspid valves come from AV canal cushions; aortic and pulmonary valves from outflow tract cushions.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Aortic and pulmonary valves derive from endocardial cushions of the outflow tract; mitral and tricuspid valves derive from fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal.
-  Clinical Findings: Valvular anomalies may be stenotic, regurgitant, atretic (tricuspid atresia), or displaced (Ebstein anomaly).
-  Diagnostics: Fetal echocardiography.
-  Management: Treatment depends on the lesion.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with sharp chest pain that worsens with inspiration and improves when he leans forward, and he also has aching pain in the left shoulder and neck. Temperature is 37.8°C and a friction rub is heard along the left sternal border. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Which of the following nerves most likely carries the pericardial pain that is referred to his shoulder?
option_A: Phrenic nerve
correct_explanation: Sharp pleuritic pain relieved by leaning forward, a friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression indicate acute pericarditis. The pericardium is innervated by the phrenic nerve. Pericarditis can cause referred pain to the neck, arms, or one or both shoulders (often left) because phrenic afferents share central pathways with those dermatomes. The pericardium consists of three layers from outer to inner: the fibrous pericardium, the parietal pericardium, and the epicardium (visceral pericardium), with the pericardial space between the parietal pericardium and epicardium.

B.reason: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart and does not carry pericardial pain. Its branch, the recurrent laryngeal nerve, can be compressed by an enlarged left atrium.

C.reason: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates the vocal cords and is compressed in Ortner syndrome. It does not mediate pericardial pain.

D.reason: The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior and does not carry pericardial sensation.

E.reason: Intercostal nerves innervate the chest wall and parietal pleura, which would produce localized pleuritic pain, not referred shoulder pain from the pericardium.

high_yield_pearl: The pericardium is innervated by the phrenic nerve; pericarditis refers pain to the shoulder and neck.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Pericardium has three layers (fibrous, parietal, epicardium/visceral); innervated by the phrenic nerve; pericarditis can cause referred pain to the neck, arms, or one or both shoulders (often left).
-  Clinical Findings: Pleuritic pain relieved by sitting forward, friction rub.
-  Diagnostics: ECG, echocardiography.
-  Management: NSAID plus colchicine.

concept_name: Coronary blood supply: left anterior descending artery
stem: A 57-year-old man presents with 2 hours of chest pressure. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1–V4 with Q waves developing in V1–V3. Echocardiography shows akinesis of the anterior wall, the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum, and the anterolateral papillary muscle. Angiography shows a proximal occlusion of the vessel that is the most commonly occluded coronary artery. Which of the following vessels is occluded?
option_A: Left anterior descending artery
correct_explanation: ST elevation in V1–V4 with akinesis of the anterior wall, anterior two thirds of the septum, and the anterolateral papillary muscle indicates an anterior infarction. The LAD and its branches supply the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum, the anterolateral papillary muscle, and the anterior surface of the LV, and it is the most commonly occluded coronary artery. The PDA, by contrast, supplies the posterior one third of the septum and the posteromedial papillary muscle. In anteroseptal infarcts, the leads V1–V2 show changes, and in anteroapical infarcts V3–V4.

B.reason: The RCA supplies the right ventricle and, in right-dominant hearts, gives the PDA, causing inferior infarction. This patient has anterior changes.

C.reason: The LCX supplies the lateral wall and causes ST elevation in I and aVL. It is not the artery to the anterior septum.

D.reason: The PDA supplies the posterior one third of the septum and the posteromedial papillary muscle. Its occlusion causes inferior or posterior infarction.

E.reason: The acute marginal artery supplies the right ventricle. Its occlusion does not cause an anterior left ventricular infarct.

high_yield_pearl: The LAD supplies the anterior 2/3 of the septum and the anterolateral papillary muscle, and is the most commonly occluded artery.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: LAD and its branches supply the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum, anterolateral papillary muscle, and anterior surface of the LV; most commonly occluded.
-  Clinical Findings: Anteroseptal (V1–V2) and anteroapical (V3–V4) ST elevation.
-  Diagnostics: ECG, angiography.
-  Management: Reperfusion, preferably PCI.

concept_name: Cardiac output variables: factors increasing stroke volume
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation has an echocardiogram for an innocent murmur. Her resting heart rate is 84/min and her blood pressure is 102/58 mm Hg. Her stroke volume is about 30% higher than before pregnancy, and her ejection fraction and arterial pressures are unchanged. Plasma volume has expanded by about 40%. Which of the following determinants of stroke volume best explains the rise?
option_A: Increased preload
correct_explanation: Stroke volume is affected by contractility, afterload, and preload (SV CAP). SV increases with increased contractility (eg, anxiety, exercise), increased preload (eg, early pregnancy), and decreased afterload. In this patient, the expansion of plasma volume raises venous return and end-diastolic volume, which raises preload. Preload is approximated by end-diastolic volume and depends on venous tone and circulating blood volume. Her arterial pressure and EF are unchanged, so the rise reflects preload and not a change in afterload or contractility.

B.reason: Increased afterload would decrease stroke volume, and her arterial pressures are not elevated. It does not explain the rise.

C.reason: Decreased contractility would lower stroke volume and ejection fraction. Her EF is unchanged.

D.reason: Decreased venous return would lower preload and stroke volume. Her blood volume is expanded, so venous return is increased.

E.reason: Heart rate affects cardiac output but not stroke volume directly. The question concerns stroke volume, and the determinants are preload, afterload, and contractility.

high_yield_pearl: SV CAP: stroke volume rises with increased contractility and preload (eg, early pregnancy) or decreased afterload.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: SV is affected by Contractility, Afterload, and Preload (SV CAP); increased with increased contractility (anxiety, exercise), increased preload (early pregnancy), decreased afterload.
-  Clinical Findings: Stroke work = SV x MAP; a failing heart has decreased SV.
-  Diagnostics: Echocardiography.
-  Management: Not applicable.

concept_name: Cardiac oxygen demand: coronary sinus oxygen content
stem: A 52-year-old man undergoes diagnostic cardiac catheterization to calculate myocardial oxygen extraction. Blood samples are taken from the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava, the right atrium, the pulmonary artery, and the coronary sinus. Arterial oxygen saturation is 98%. Which of the following samples is expected to have the lowest oxygen content?
option_A: Coronary sinus
correct_explanation: The myocardium extracts a very large fraction of the oxygen delivered by the coronary arteries, even at rest. The coronary sinus drains the cardiac veins and therefore contains the most deoxygenated blood in the body. Myocardial oxygen demand is increased by contractility, afterload, heart rate, and ventricular diameter (wall tension). Mixed venous blood sampled in the pulmonary artery has a higher saturation because it combines blood from all tissues, including those with lower extraction. The coronary sinus saturation is therefore the lowest.

B.reason: The SVC carries blood from the upper body, which has a moderate saturation. It is higher than coronary sinus blood.

C.reason: The IVC carries blood from the lower body, including the kidneys, which extract little oxygen, so its saturation is relatively high.

D.reason: The pulmonary artery carries mixed venous blood that includes the coronary sinus return diluted with other sources. Its saturation is higher than that of the coronary sinus.

E.reason: The right atrium receives blood from the SVC, IVC, and coronary sinus, so it is an average of these and is higher than the coronary sinus alone.

high_yield_pearl: The coronary sinus holds the most deoxygenated blood in the body.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Myocardial O2 demand is increased by contractility, afterload (proportional to arterial pressure), heart rate, and ventricular diameter (wall tension); coronary sinus contains the most deoxygenated blood in the body.
-  Clinical Findings: High extraction means increased demand must be met by increased flow.
-  Diagnostics: Oxygen saturation sampling during catheterization.
-  Management: Reduce O2 demand in angina.

concept_name: Cardiac output: effect of tachycardia on diastolic filling
stem: A 61-year-old man with a prior MI presents with lightheadedness and a blood pressure of 78/50 mm Hg. ECG shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 218/min, and his cardiac output is markedly reduced. His stroke volume at rest was 75 mL and is now estimated at 25 mL. Which of the following best explains the fall in cardiac output at this heart rate?
option_A: Shortened diastole reduces ventricular filling time and stroke volume
option_D: Increased venous return from sympathetic activation
correct_explanation: A regular wide-complex tachycardia at 218/min in a patient with a prior MI is ventricular tachycardia. Cardiac output is the product of stroke volume and heart rate, and in early exercise it is maintained by increases in both. At very high heart rates, diastole is shortened more than systole, so diastolic filling time falls and stroke volume falls. When stroke volume decreases proportionally more than rate increases, cardiac output falls, as in this patient. This is why ventricular tachycardia can cause hypotension and syncope.

B.reason: Increased afterload could lower stroke volume, but there is no evidence of vasoconstriction, and his hypotension reflects a fall in output. The classic mechanism in rapid tachycardia is reduced filling.

C.reason: Acidosis decreases contractility but would be a late consequence and is not the primary mechanism. The shortened filling time at 218/min is the dominant factor.

D.reason: Sympathetic activation increases venous return in general but cannot compensate for the loss of filling time at this heart rate.

E.reason: Prolonged systole would not occur at such a high rate, and ejection fraction is not the mechanism. Diastole, not systole, is what shortens most.

high_yield_pearl: At very high heart rates, diastolic filling time falls, decreasing stroke volume and cardiac output.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: CO = SV x HR; in early exercise, CO is maintained by increased HR and SV; later by increased HR only (SV plateaus); diastole is shortened with very high HR (eg, VT), decreasing diastolic filling time, SV, and CO.
-  Clinical Findings: Hypotension, syncope in VT.
-  Diagnostics: ECG.
-  Management: Cardioversion if unstable.

stem: A 33-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle collision with an estimated 1,000-mL blood loss. Blood pressure is 96/70 mm Hg and heart rate is 118/min, and his veins are collapsed. The trauma physician explains that sympathetic venoconstriction helps maintain venous return by mobilizing stored blood. Which of the following vessel types accounts for most of the blood storage capacity of the circulation?
option_A: Veins
correct_explanation: Veins provide most of the blood storage capacity of the circulation because they are highly compliant. Sympathetic venoconstriction reduces venous capacity, shifting stored blood centrally to maintain venous return and preload after hemorrhage. Arterioles, in contrast, account for most of the total peripheral resistance, and capillaries have the highest total cross-sectional area and the lowest flow velocity. This explains how a patient can tolerate moderate blood loss with only mild hypotension. The vascular function curve shifts with changes in venous tone and volume.

B.reason: Arterioles account for most of TPR and regulate blood pressure and regional flow, but they hold a small fraction of the blood volume.

C.reason: Capillaries have the highest total cross-sectional area and lowest velocity, which favors exchange, but they contain a small volume.

D.reason: The aorta is a high-pressure conduit with low compliance relative to veins and stores little blood.

E.reason: Pulmonary arteries hold a modest volume and are not the main storage site of the systemic circulation.

high_yield_pearl: Veins provide most blood storage capacity; arterioles provide most resistance.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Arterioles account for most of TPR; veins provide most of the blood storage capacity; capillaries have the highest total cross-sectional area and lowest flow velocity.
-  Clinical Findings: Venoconstriction shifts blood centrally after hemorrhage.
-  Diagnostics: Hemodynamic monitoring.
-  Management: Volume resuscitation.

stem: A 23-year-old medical student is learning to correlate auscultation with the cardiac cycle on a healthy volunteer. The instructor points out the first and second heart sounds and asks the student to identify the valve events producing them. The volunteer is in sinus rhythm at 68/min with no murmurs. Which of the following valve events produces the second heart sound, and where is it loudest?
option_A: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves, loudest at the left upper sternal border
option_B: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, loudest at the mitral area
option_C: Opening of the mitral valve, loudest at the apex
option_D: Rapid ventricular filling, loudest at the apex in left lateral decubitus
option_E: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle, loudest at the apex
correct_explanation: S1 is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves and is loudest at the mitral area. S2 is produced by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves and is loudest at the left upper sternal border. S2 marks the end of ventricular systole and the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation. S3 occurs in early diastole during rapid filling and S4 in late diastole with atrial kick. Splitting of S2 results from the physiologic delay of pulmonic closure during inspiration.

B.reason: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves produces S1, which is loudest at the mitral area, not S2.

C.reason: Opening of the mitral valve is normally silent, but in mitral stenosis it produces an opening snap after S2. It is not the origin of S2.

D.reason: Rapid ventricular filling produces an S3 in early diastole, best heard at the apex in left lateral decubitus. It is not normally audible in healthy adults.

E.reason: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle produces an S4 in late diastole. It is abnormal if palpable.

high_yield_pearl: S1 = mitral and tricuspid closure; S2 = aortic and pulmonic closure (loudest at the left upper sternal border).
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: S1: mitral and tricuspid closure, loudest at the mitral area; S2: aortic and pulmonary closure, loudest at the LUSB; S3: early diastole rapid filling; S4: late diastole atrial kick.
-  Clinical Findings: Pathologic S3 and S4 indicate volume overload and stiff ventricle, respectively.
-  Diagnostics: Auscultation with correlation to the cardiac cycle.
-  Management: Not applicable.

stem: A 31-year-old man who injects heroin presents with 5 days of fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain, and cough. Temperature is 39.4°C and heart rate is 118/min, and a holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Chest radiograph shows multiple peripheral nodular opacities with cavitation, and transthoracic echocardiography shows a large vegetation on the tricuspid valve. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
option_A: Staphylococcus aureus
correct_explanation: Fever, a tricuspid regurgitation murmur, septic pulmonary emboli with cavitation, and a tricuspid vegetation in an injection drug user indicate right-sided infective endocarditis. Tricuspid valve involvement is associated with injection drug use (don't 'tri' drugs). Right-sided vegetations embolize to the lungs, whereas left-sided vegetations embolize to the systemic circulation. In injection drug users, the common organisms are S aureus, Pseudomonas, and Candida, and S aureus is the classic cause of acute endocarditis with large destructive vegetations.

B.reason: Viridans streptococci cause subacute endocarditis on previously damaged valves after dental procedures. This patient has an acute presentation on the tricuspid valve.

C.reason: Enterococcus is associated with GI or GU procedures, not injection drug use, and usually affects left-sided valves.

D.reason: Staphylococcus epidermidis is associated with prosthetic valves. This patient has a native tricuspid valve.

E.reason: Coxiella is a cause of culture-negative endocarditis in patients with animal exposure. This patient has a typical acute presentation from drug use.

high_yield_pearl: IV drug use: right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis, usually S aureus, with septic pulmonary emboli.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Endothelial injury leads to vegetations of platelets, fibrin, and microbes; acute: S aureus (high virulence, large destructive vegetations on normal valves). Tricuspid valve involvement is associated with injection drug use; right-sided emboli go to the lungs, left-sided to the systemic circulation.
-  Clinical Findings: Fever, new murmur, vascular and immunologic phenomena.
-  Diagnostics: Multiple blood cultures and echocardiography.
-  Management: Antibiotics; surgery for complications.

stem: A 45-year-old sheep farmer has had 6 weeks of low-grade fevers, night sweats, and fatigue. Temperature is 38.0°C, and he has clubbing and a new holosystolic apical murmur. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on a previously abnormal mitral valve. Six sets of blood cultures incubated for 7 days are negative, and he has not received antibiotics. His farm had lambing-associated animal exposure several months ago. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
option_A: Coxiella burnetii
correct_explanation: Persistent fever, clubbing, a new regurgitant murmur, and a mitral vegetation with repeatedly negative blood cultures indicate culture-negative infective endocarditis. First Aid lists Coxiella and Bartonella as the culture-negative organisms, and animal exposure such as lambing makes Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) the most likely cause. Common associations include S aureus with injection drug use, S epidermidis with prosthetic valves, Enterococcus with GI or GU procedures, S gallolyticus with colon cancer, and HACEK organisms for Gram-negative cases. The diagnosis requires multiple blood cultures and echocardiography.

B.reason: S aureus grows readily in blood cultures and causes an acute illness with large vegetations. This patient's cultures are negative and his course is subacute.

C.reason: Viridans streptococci grow in standard cultures and are associated with dental procedures, so negative cultures argue against them.

D.reason: S gallolyticus grows in blood cultures and is associated with colon cancer. This patient's cultures are negative.

E.reason: Pseudomonas is seen in injection drug users and grows in standard cultures. It would not cause negative cultures.

high_yield_pearl: Culture-negative endocarditis: Coxiella and Bartonella.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Endothelial injury leads to vegetations; associations: prosthetic valves (S epidermidis), GI/GU procedures (Enterococcus), colon cancer (S gallolyticus), Gram-negative (HACEK organisms: Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), culture-negative (Coxiella, Bartonella), injection drug use (S aureus, Pseudomonas, Candida).
-  Clinical Findings: Fever, new murmur, vascular and immunologic phenomena.
-  Diagnostics: Multiple blood cultures, echocardiography; serology for culture-negative organisms.
-  Management: Targeted antibiotics; evaluate the source.

stem: A 62-year-old man undergoing an open colectomy develops a narrow-complex tachycardia at 168/min with a blood pressure of 112/68 mm Hg. He has well-controlled asthma and is on a ventilator, and the anesthesiologist wants a rate-control agent that can be titrated quickly and that will wear off within minutes if bronchospasm or hypotension develops. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
option_A: Esmolol
correct_explanation: A perioperative supraventricular tachycardia in a patient with reactive airway disease requires a rate-controlling drug that is rapidly reversible. Class II beta-blockers (metoprolol, propranolol, esmolol, atenolol, timolol, carvedilol) decrease SA and AV nodal activity by decreasing cAMP and Ca2+ currents, suppress abnormal pacemakers by decreasing the slope of phase 4, and prolong the PR interval. Esmolol is very short acting, so any adverse effect such as hypotension or bronchospasm dissipates within minutes of stopping the infusion. The other options are longer acting and could not be quickly withdrawn.

B.reason: Atenolol is a longer-acting beta-blocker given orally or intravenously for hours. Its effects cannot be quickly reversed if bronchospasm develops.

C.reason: Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker with beta-2 effects that can cause bronchoconstriction in asthma and has a longer duration of action.

D.reason: Carvedilol is a nonselective beta-blocker with alpha-blocking activity used mainly in heart failure. It is oral and long acting and is not suited to acute titration.

E.reason: Timolol is a nonselective, longer-acting beta-blocker that carries bronchospasm risk and cannot be rapidly titrated.

high_yield_pearl: Esmolol is the very short-acting beta-blocker for rapid titration.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Class II beta-blockers decrease SA and AV nodal activity by decreasing cAMP and Ca2+ currents; suppress abnormal pacemakers by decreasing the slope of phase 4; AV node is particularly sensitive (PR interval prolongs); esmolol is very short acting.
-  Clinical Findings: Uses: SVT, ventricular rate control for AF and flutter, prevent ventricular arrhythmia post-MI.
-  Diagnostics: ECG; blood pressure monitoring.
-  Management: Adverse effects: bradycardia, AV block, HF, bronchospasm in asthma and COPD.

concept_name: Antiarrhythmics: class I sodium channel blockers and use dependence
stem: A 59-year-old man with ventricular ectopy is started on a class I antiarrhythmic. His cardiologist notes that the drug suppresses ectopic beats at his rapid ventricular rate of 150/min during exercise more effectively than at his resting rate of 60/min. His ECG at rest shows a QRS duration of 96 msec. Which of the following best explains the rate-dependent effect of the drug?
option_A: At faster rates, diastole is shorter, so Na+ channels spend less time in the resting state and the drug has less time to dissociate
option_B: At faster rates, the drug binds more avidly to resting channels
option_C: At faster rates, K+ channels are blocked more effectively
option_D: At slower rates, the drug is metabolized more quickly
option_E: At faster rates, calcium channels are blocked more effectively
correct_explanation: Class I antiarrhythmics slow or block conduction, especially in depolarized cells, by decreasing the slope of phase 0 depolarization. Their action is increased at faster heart rates, a property called state dependence or use dependence. At a faster rate, diastole is shorter, so Na+ channels spend less time in the resting state, and the drugs dissociate from the receptor during this state, giving them less time to dissociate. The block therefore accumulates, and the effect is most pronounced with class IC, then IA, then IB drugs because of relative binding strength (Fast taxi CAB).

B.reason: Class I drugs bind preferentially to open or inactivated channels, not resting channels. Dissociation occurs during the resting state, which is why short diastole increases block.

C.reason: K+ channel blockade is the mechanism of class III agents and not of class I sodium channel blockers.

D.reason: Metabolism of the drug is not rate dependent and does not explain use-dependent block.

E.reason: Calcium channel blockade is the mechanism of class IV drugs and is unrelated to class I use dependence.

high_yield_pearl: Class I drugs are use dependent: more block at faster rates because there is less time for the drug to dissociate.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Class I sodium channel blockers slow or block conduction, especially in depolarized cells; decrease slope of phase 0; increased action at faster HR (state dependent); effect most pronounced in IC > IA > IB (Fast taxi CAB).
-  Clinical Findings: IA: quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide; IB: lidocaine, mexiletine; IC: flecainide, propafenone.
-  Diagnostics: ECG QRS duration.
-  Management: Choose by arrhythmia and structural heart disease.

stem: A pathologist examines the heart of a 26-week fetus with trisomy 18 after pregnancy termination. The specimen shows a normal ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk that arise as two separate vessels, with a ventricular septal defect. She reviews the normal derivation of the great vessels to classify the defect. Which of the following embryonic structures gives rise to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk?
option_A: Truncus arteriosus
correct_explanation: The truncus arteriosus gives rise to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. The truncal and bulbar ridges, formed by neural crest cell migrations, spiral and fuse to form the aorticopulmonary septum, which divides the truncus into these two vessels. By contrast, the bulbus cordis forms the smooth outflow parts of the ventricles, the primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated parts, and the endocardial cushions form the atrial septum, membranous interventricular septum, and AV and semilunar valves. The normal separation of the great vessels in this specimen indicates that the truncal division was intact and that the VSD arises from another failure.

B.reason: The bulbus cordis forms the smooth outflow tracts of the ventricles, not the great vessels themselves.

C.reason: The endocardial cushions give rise to the atrial septum, membranous interventricular septum, and AV and semilunar valves. They do not form the vessel walls.

D.reason: The primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated portions of the left and right ventricles.

E.reason: The sinus venosus horns form the smooth part of the right atrium and the coronary sinus, and not the great arteries.

high_yield_pearl: Truncus arteriosus gives the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Truncus arteriosus: ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk; bulbus cordis: smooth outflow tracts of LV and RV; primitive ventricle: trabeculated LV and RV; endocardial cushion: atrial septum, membranous IV septum, AV and semilunar valves.
-  Clinical Findings: Neural crest failure causes persistent truncus, TGA, and tetralogy of Fallot.
-  Diagnostics: Fetal echocardiography.
-  Management: Surgical repair after birth for significant lesions.

concept_name: Fetal circulation: path of superior vena cava blood
stem: A fetal echocardiographer is tracing the circulation of a 32-week fetus. She observes that blood returning from the head and upper body via the superior vena cava enters the right atrium and is directed through the tricuspid valve rather than across the interatrial septum. The fetal pulmonary arteries show high resistance, and a vessel connecting the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta is open. Which of the following describes the subsequent path of this deoxygenated blood?
option_A: Right ventricle, main pulmonary artery, ductus arteriosus, descending aorta
option_B: Right atrium, foramen ovale, left atrium, ascending aorta
option_C: Right ventricle, pulmonary veins, left atrium
option_D: Right atrium, ductus venosus, inferior vena cava
correct_explanation: In the fetal circulation, deoxygenated blood from the SVC enters the right atrium and flows into the right ventricle and the main pulmonary artery. Because of the high fetal pulmonary artery resistance, most of this blood is shunted through the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta rather than through the lungs. In contrast, most of the highly oxygenated blood from the IVC crosses the foramen ovale to the left atrium. The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood through the ductus venosus into the IVC, bypassing the hepatic circulation. After birth, the lower pulmonary resistance reverses these shunts.

B.reason: The foramen ovale directs the more oxygenated IVC blood, not SVC blood, to the left atrium. SVC blood streams preferentially through the tricuspid valve.

C.reason: Blood does not return through pulmonary veins from the right ventricle without passing through the lungs, and little blood passes through the fetal lungs.

D.reason: The ductus venosus carries umbilical venous blood into the IVC. It does not receive blood from the right atrium.

E.reason: The umbilical arteries arise from the internal iliac arteries and carry fetal blood to the placenta, not directly from the right ventricle.

high_yield_pearl: Fetal SVC blood goes RA, RV, pulmonary artery, ductus arteriosus, descending aorta because of high pulmonary resistance.
topic_overview:
-  Etiology/Pathophysiology: Three fetal shunts: umbilical vein, ductus venosus, IVC (bypasses liver); IVC blood, foramen ovale, LA; SVC blood, RA, RV, pulmonary artery, ductus arteriosus, descending aorta (due to high fetal pulmonary resistance).
-  Clinical Findings: At birth, decreased pulmonary resistance closes the foramen ovale; increased O2 and decreased prostaglandins close the ductus.
-  Diagnostics: Fetal echocardiography.
-  Management: NSAIDs or acetaminophen to close a PDA; PGE keeps it open.

stem: A 20-year-old man with an unrepaired coarctation of the aorta, diagnosed incidentally at age 12 but lost to follow-up, presents with the sudden onset of the worst headache of his life followed by brief loss of consciousness. Blood pressure is 176/104 mm Hg in the right arm, femoral pulses are weak, and he has nuchal rigidity. Noncontrast head CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his intracranial hemorrhage?
option_A: Rupture of a berry aneurysm
option_C: Hypertensive hemorrhage from Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm in the basal ganglia
correct_explanation: A thunderclap headache with nuchal rigidity and blood in the basal cisterns indicates subarachnoid hemorrhage, most commonly from a ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm. In a patient with coarctation of the aorta, the complications include heart failure, an increased risk of cerebral hemorrhage (berry aneurysms), aortic rupture, and infective endocarditis. The upper extremity hypertension and weak femoral pulses confirm uncorrected coarctation. The increased risk of berry aneurysms is the key link between the vascular lesion and this presentation.

B.reason: A mycotic aneurysm is an infective complication of endocarditis, and this patient has no fever or endocarditis findings. Berry aneurysm is the listed association in coarctation.
